Mr. HUGH GUTHRIE (South Wellington) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 25) in further amendment of the Railway Act.
He said : As the matter dealt with in this proposed amendment is somewhat involved, this may be as suitable a time as any to offer a few words in explanation of the scope of the Bill. The object of the Bill is, if not to prohibit, at least very greatly to limit the power of a railway company operating under a Dominion charter to contract itself out of its common-law or statutory liabilities to its employees in the case of injury resulting from the negligence of the company or its servants. The whole trend of modern legislation upon this point, as regards employers and employees, is strongly in the direction of safeguarding the right of the workman, and to prevent any contract or agreement from proving a bar or hindrance to the recovery of compensation by the workman. While the Bill which I have asked leave to introduce is wide in its terms, and will, if passed, affect all railway companies operating under Dominion charter, yet, as a matter of fact, the only company really concerned at the present time is the Grand Trunk Railway Company. This arises from the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway has, in years past, obtained certain special legislation from the parliament of Canada, and I have not been able to ascertain that any other railway company enjoys similar privileges.

Tlie difficulty which it is sought to remedy had its origin as far back as 1874, when the Grand Trunk Railway Company obtained the passage of an Act to enable them to set aside a fund, and to form a superannuation and provident society for its workmen. They were entitled, under this Act of 1874, to formulate a scheme, to formulate rules for the transaction of the business of the society, and for the government of the members of the society. In 1878, they obtained further legislation authorizing them, in addition to their superannuation fund and provident fund, to establish an accident and life insurance fund, and to conduct the business of life insurance and accident insurance, with regard to their workmen, and in connection with their superannuation society.
Then in 1880, the Great Western Railway Company obtained similar legislation. In 1884, after amalgamation of the two roads, this superannuation and insurance society was applied to the whole system of the Grand Trunk Railway. This was again confirmed by an Act of 1888. Now the difficulty which presents itself is this : Under authority of these various special Acts the Grand Trunk Railway Company has formed a society known as the Grand Trunk Railway Insurance and Provident Society. They have passed rules, regulations and by-laws for the government of the society and the members of the society. Rule number 5 provides that every workman, the moment he enters into the employment of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, becomes a member of that society, and is bound by its laws. Rule 66 provides that all rules and regulations of the society shall be submitted to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and approved by them. But the most objectionable1 rule, or by-law, of the society is by-law 15, and it is under that by-law that the difficulty arises. Bylaw number 15 provides :
In consideration of the subscription of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to this society, no member thereof or his representatives shall have any claim against the company for compensation on account of injury or death from accident.
Under these various Acts the railway is empowered to grant certain money to this fund. I have heard it stated in open court that they do grant annually $12,500, and as they have approximately 25,000 workmen, they pay 50 cents for each man into that fund, and as a result they claim they have absolute protection from all common law or statutory liability towards there workmen. Now they do provide some insurance, but they charge the workmen for the insurance at the rate of 40 or 50 cents a month; for the vast majority of their 25,000 men the rate is 50 cents per month, or $6 per year. For this they provide, in case of sickness, an indemnity of $3 per week for 26 weeks in the case of permanent disability, a sum of $100; and in the case of death, a sum of $250. They do not give
as much as can be obtained by workmen doing similar work, from any one of the score of friendly or benevolent societies doing business in Canada to-day.
Now this matter has lain dormant for many years. I think it is only within the last eighteen months that the question has really arisen. During that period it has been 'decided by a trial judge in the province of Quebec, by a trial judge in the province of Ontario, and I think likewise by a trial judge in the province of British Columbia, that under that by-law 15 the workman is absolutely precluded from recovering against the railway company, even in case of the negligence of the company or of its servants. If I were to venture my own opinion in the matter, I would have no hesitation myself in saying that by-law 15 is not authorized by any enabling of the Acts ; but it has been decided otherwise by trial judges. The difficulty of the situation is this, that where you have as plaintiff a disabled or injured railway man, or the widow of a deceased railway man, they are not in a position to carry this matter further and get the decision of a higher court upon it. As long as the matter is involved in doubt, or as long as the present decision stands, these 25,000 workmen in that company are absolutely debarred from recovering damages against the company in cases of Injury resulting from negligence. The Bill which I have brought in is framed largely on the lines of clause 10 of the Ontario Workmen's Compensation Act and a similar clause is to be found in the English Act, the Employers Liability Act, and no doubt in other provincial Acts with which I am not familiar. It does not preclude agreements between the employers and their employees, but it simply provides that no agreement shall be allowed to prevail as a defense unless, in the first place, there is consideration on the part of the workman for entering into such an agreement other than the mere fact of his being taken into the employment ; and unless the agreement is reasonable, just and adequate in the opinion of the judge who tries the case ; and unless, in the opinion of the judge who tries the case, it is not improvident on the part of the workman. The onus of establishing the reasonableness and the adequacy of the consideration is thrown upon the railway company. That, Mr. Speaker, is in brief the Bill which I ask leave to introduce this afternoon.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I desire to say that I made some inquiry a few days ago about some matters moved for in the House, and so far as I know they have not been brought down yet. I am particularly anxious to get the correspondence between the depart-

rnent and Mr. Devlin relative to what lie said about members of this House, also about the number of immigrants that were brought to this country for the last ten years, also about a report with reference to the work of the Experimental Farm, also with reference to the Belleville post office and the dismissals that took place there.

Yes.

speechtext: We have bought a site for the building. The plans are prepared, tenders are now being called for, and in a few weeks they will be in.

speechtext: Would the Minister of Finance please tell us for what other purposes besides a customs-house ?

While the main purpose is to transfer the customhouse from the present building to the new one, other public purposes of the city of Halifax will of course be served by it. If there should be any spare rooms, some other branches of the service may be placed there. While it is called a custom-house building the department would not want to confine it absolutely to customs purposes if any other branch could be accommodated within the same building.

No, tenders are called for.	.
New Brunswick-Marysville public building, $9,500.
What is this building for?
This work is under contract now, the contractors being the Messrs. Simmons, and the contract price is $6,842. Besides that we have paid $1,000 for the site, and there is the fitting up and so on.
Is that the total cost of the building ?
Yes, the whole cost of the building.
What is the population of Marysville ?
Marysville is a thriving town in New Brunswick. The population, which is increasing every day

The population is about
2,000.
And increasing rapidly.

And increasing rapidly. A lot of people are coming from outside towns to work there. Abo.ut 600 people work in the cotton factory there who live a mile or two away. We have supplied the government with a building for post office purposes for the last 35 years, and I think we are entitled to a post office.
What is the estimated Mr. CLANCY. I would like to ask the cost of this building ?	hon. Minister of Public Works whether the

lion, gentleman or the government has some fixed policy in expending money without taking into consideration only the population and the general prospects of the place. It is a very easy matter now for any hon. gentleman to state that he has a thriving village or town ; in fact, if my memory serves me, the hon. Minister of Public Works always has a thriving town where he is putting up a building. Perhaps it would be convenient for the non. gentleman to state whether he has any policy upon the question of putting up any public buildings in all the small towns and villages in Canada. If that gate is opened I am sure there are many hon. members on both sides of the House will be able to supply a similar reason ; if it is not open, the hon. gentleman should explain why he has given this reason.

In former years there was in this parliament a gentleman who was the Minister of Finance in a Conservative administration. That gentleman was called the Hon. George E. Foster. He was representing the riding of York, New Brunswick, and when he was the member for that riding he placed in the estimates an amount of money for the erection of a public building at Marysville. I have simply inherited the obligation of expending that sum of money. .1 am spending it. I hope that I will spend less than Mr. Foster would have done, because he was known to be a very expensive man. In other words, joking apart, I found in the estimates when we took office a sum of money for the erection of a building at Marysville. Now, I am simply carrying out the pledge that was given under the late administration, and the wisdom of which I fully recognize.

The hon. gentleman's memory appears to be very clear about one part of it, but there is another part of it which the bon. gentleman has forgotten. Does the hon. minister not know from the same source that he obtained the information in regard to an estimate being put in for that public building at Marysville when Mr. Foster was Minister of Finance and represented the riding of York, that the people of Marysville were to contribute half the cost of the building ? It was explained to this House on a former occasion that the people of this town or village, whichever it may be, were to contribute a portion towards the erection of a public building there. Now, the hon. gentleman states that he has undertaken the whole cost, so that he will find no reason for the explanation he has given in the promise that was made in the past, as the circumstances are different. He should now offer some explanation of his policy.

There is no trace in my department of any * promise or engagement whatever by which
I
the town of Marysville undertook to pay half the cost of the building.

I have never heard of any promise being made such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has referred to, to contribute half of the cost of a public building at Marysville. I think if there is any place in the Dominion of Canada that deserves a public building, it is Marysville. We have a large cotton mill which gives employment to 750 hands and we pay out in wages $45,000 a month. This is not n village; it is the town of Marysville of which I have the honour to be mayor.

I understand the hon. Minister of Public Works to give as a reason for this estimate that the Hon. George E. Foster had made an appropriation while he was in office. I do not understand the hon. minister to give us any other reason for placing this amount in the estimates. The information I understand this committee to desire from the hon. minister is the ground upon which he can justify the expenditure of this money.

I think that my hon. friends are a little too exacting in asking for reasons now, for erecting a building which was approved by their friends in office when a vote is placed in the estimates. While I do not hesitate to say that it is a good thing to have public buildings in thriving towns and villages provided they are not too expensive, yet we must not spend too much. It shows that we are progressing and it gives confidence to the country. I believe it is a good argument to say that when the faith of the country has been pledged by the late administration, as far as it could, we should recognize that pledge when we think it was wise to give it.

It is very extraordinary that the minister will not answer the question put to him. The minister cannot say that since he has presided over the Department of Public Works he has carried out all the grants that were put in the estimates by the former government. Therefore, his argument on that score does not amount to much. If the hon. gentleman says that he is making a special exception in this case that might be an answer to the question put to him ; but if he is not making a special exception in this instance, then we desire to know if it is the policy of the government to erect public buildings in all towns similar to this. Th'e hon. gentleman knows that this policy will lead to a very great expenditure. There is no hon. gentleman on either side of the House who would not think it very nice to have a public building in the principle town of his riding ; but, if the Minister of Public Works commences to pick up places here and there we will have a just cause to complain. If the hon. gentleman carries out that policy then I can present to him a couple of places

where the reasons for the erection of a public building are quite as strong as they are in Marysville.
Each case should be judged on its own merits. I do not think there is a general rule which can be applied. It depends on many things.
Politics.
Oh, no. My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) must not forget that when his party were in power there was a lot of politics done.
Oh, no.
Yes ; I did a lot of it with them.
Oh, no.

And when they are on this side of the House again they will do just the same thing ; in fact they will do worse than we do. The principles then will be the same that govern us to-day, and each case will have to be judged by itself. This is a most meritorious case. The Hon. Geo. E. Poster is a witness to that, and I cannot call a better witness to my aid. I am willing to say that we must not erect too many public buildings. But my friends do not forget that a great many public buildings were erected in the past, and we have some members on this side of the House that have their two eyes open to the magnificent public buildings that were erected in the Conservative days. They have placed their claims before me and if I were not an energetic man I would have to ask for a great deal more money than I ask now. But I face the music manfully, and I only decide to give money to meritorious cases like this one.

When I mentioned the word ' politics ' I had in mind the arguments used by the supporters of the government when they were in opposition and which were very similar to the arguments used by my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) to-day. The Liberals when in opposition charged the Conservatives with allowing party politics to have more to do with the investment of money in public buildings than the circumstances would warrant. The principle pursued by the Con servative government is being pursued today by the present government. If it was wrong then it is wrong now, and if it was right then it is right now.
It was right then.
Oh, very well.

Has the site been purchased for this building ?
The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS Yes.	I

No.

One thousand dollars, which has been paid.

The whole town ? The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS. Nobody can buy a piece of land outside of them.

Richibucto public building, $5,000.
'Mr. CLARKE. Is this as meritorious as the other case ?
Well, 1 should think so. The site has been bought for $805 and we intend to erect a commodious and cheap building costing about $6,000.

3,986 souls. It Is a large town.

What public buildings is this vote for ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS The customs-house, the post office and savings bank.

The amount which is voted in the estimates.
St. John immigrant building, $10,000.
What is this building for?

For immigration purposes. During the present winter, although the building is not completed, we have had several thousand immigrants in it. My hon. friend does not forget, I am sure, that St. John is a terminus of the Canadian Pacific Railway, it is our winter port, and the building is a most useful one.
How much has been spent on that building altogether ?
About $33,000 all completed.
Including the site ?
Oh, yes.
What has the site cost ?
It has been given to us by the city.
Is the building being built under contract, and if so, what is the name of the contractor ?
Yes, by J. H. Pullen, of St. John.
Is there an immigrant building in Halifax ?
Oh, yes.
What did it cost ?
I cannot give the exact cost of it to-day. If my hon. friend wants the information, I will take a note of it, and give it to him later.
May I ask what the exact purpose of the building is ? Do you keep the immigrants there for a short time after their arrival, or is it for shelter ?
Yes. Some ships which have arrived there during the past winter have carried a thousand immigrants.
Were they for the United States or for Canada ?
Some for Canada and some for the United States.

In return for the accommodation afforded to immigrants going through to the United States does the government require the steamship companies carrying them to pay part of the cost of the maintenance of this building; or is it the policy of the government to pay ail the cost, both of erecting the building and of maintaining it for the accommodation of these people ?

In the past the transportation companies have not been called ujion to pay any share of the maintenance of the building. I admit that the immigrant trade, if I may call it so, is a good one for our transportation companies and for our towns and cities. It is a trade, just as much as any other trade; and thus far the government have not asked the transportation companies to contribute anything towards the erection of these sheds. St. John being a winter port, the government thought it was a good thing to equip it with all the implements of civilization.
Maritime provinces generally-Dominion public buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs, etc., $12,000.
How much was expended last year ?
Quebec-Dominion public buildings, renewals, improvements, repairs, etc., $12,000.
This is the same vote as before.
How is that divided ?
This vote is spread all over the country, in various small sums of $300 or $500, for repairs which are not of such importance as to call for a special vote in the estimates.
Would the minister state how much was expended in Montreal ?

On the Montreal custom-house $59.25; on the post office, $396.50. We had a special
vote for Montreal.
Mr; MONK. Are we supposed to spend that sum every year-$12,000-neither more nor less ?
Yes, and generally we are short.
I know that apart from this you vote special sums for repairs in Montreal, Quebec and other places.

Yes, other votes cover large expenditures. This vote is to cover expenditures for small repairs wherever they may be required.
Drummondville public building, $2,000.
Under contract to complete.
What will the total cost of this building be when completed ?

I think there is a great deal to support the contention of my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) that we ought to be informed what is the policy of the government in regard to these public buildings. I have no objection to the erection of a public building in Drummondville; but there are many other places in the province of Quebec which could rightly claim a public building. What are the conditions to which they have to conform ? Elect Reform candidates ? That seems to be the rule in our province. I think we are entitled to a statement from the government as to what their policy is in this regard, and what are the conditions to which parties must conform in order to obtain the erection of a public building. I heard the case of Marysville discussed a few moments ago. The hon. minister will remember that last year I called his attention very particularly to the town of St. Laurent in the county of Jacques Cartier- a large place, whose population is increasing more rapidly than that of Marysville, and where the necessity of a public building has been felt for a long time. It has very large educational institutions, is a distributing centre for postal matter and is a place which in every respect would warrant the government in erecting a public building there. My hon. friend did not fail to recognize that last year and promised to look into the matter, and I called his attention to the fact that there was a public building there, which had cost a great deal, and was available to the government at a low figure. I have no objection to a building in Drum-mondsville or Granby, but when there are other places equally as well if not better entitled to consideration, we ought to know the policy of the government. Must the localities furnish the site or any of the money and what should be the population and conditions of trade ? We should have a fixed rule, and the localities which conform to that rule should be able to obtain Hon. Mr. TARTE.
a hearing from the government. Otherwise it becomes simply a question, as the hon. minister said a moment ago, of deciding each case on a different principle, and the locality with the strongest pull is the one that will get the public building. That is a very bad policy.
We are all of the same opinion with regard to fixed rules, and that is that they are no good. There is no business man who will say that he has always acted on fixed rules.
Then general principles.

The general principle I endeavour to follow faithfully is to listen to every representation made to me and then make up my judgment without too much bias. My hon. friend is right in what he says about St. Laurent. Only we have so many things to do that we cannot do them all at once. St. Laurent is a fine village, and I have no doubt the time will come when it will have a magnificent public building. But that does not take anything from the merits of Drummondville. The merits of St. Laurent are one thing and of Drummondville another. When the building at Drummondville is completed, let us hope that within a short period we will have the pleasure of going to St. Laurent and seeing a public building there.
What is the population of Drummondville ?
Over 2,000.

What will the building cost ?
^ The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. $15,000 all told. Drummondville is a town which is coming to the front very fast indeed. There is a prosperous wave in that locality, several manufactories have been started, there is a good water power in operation, and the government of Quebec is doing a great deal to make the place progress.
What is the revenue of the post office ?

The postal revenue in 1S99 and 1900 was $2,322. There were money orders issued for over $15,000, and this year instead of $15,000, $22,000 of money orders are issued.
Granby, public building, Quebec, $11,000.
What is to be the total cost ?
Grosse Isle quarantine station, $10,000.

This is required for some extensive improvements. There were no water works or bath or electric lighting and we are equipping the station with these, as it ought to be. This

sum -will complete the work, and this station will be not only the best in this country but on the continent. I am informed that during the last five years we spent about $60,000, and a much larger amount was spent the preceding five years.
How many immigrants in the course of a year ?
Only those who are sick are quarantined there.
How many were quarantined there last year ?
We are not now on the question of quarantine, and I am only the contractor for the improvements.

I could not say off hand, how many people were quarantined, but every year a certain number must be quarantined. I have not got the data here, but will have all the information when the quarantine item comes up for discussion. In the course of a year the average is 40 or 50, but there must be accommodation for a great many more because sometimes we will have to land a shipload of immigrants, 1,200 or 1,300, at a time.
During last season one ship was quarantined which had on board over 2,000 souls.
We have spent about $60,000 for the purpose of accommodating between 40 and 50 immigrants.

That is an unfair representation of the facts because although we may not have on an average more than I have stated in a year, yet at any one time we are liable to have more than one shipload of immigrants in quarantine. On one occasion there were 2,100 people in Grosse Isle.
On the ship ?
They had to be landed on shore and were kept in quarantine for over a month.
What ship ?

I cannot remember. It was a year and a half ago. The same thing occurred at Halifax on another occasion. The two ships came in one after the other and probably over 1,500 had to be accommodated at one time or another. Generally we have nobody there but are liable any moment to have this large number coming in on us, and we must supply the accommodation.

I would like to know which of these lion, gentlemen is correct. The hon. Minister of Public Works told us that the place cost about $60,000. We asked the hon. Minister of Agriculture how many people there were retained there last year, and he did not know, but said that there were forty or fifty the year before.
What I intended to say, and what I think I did say, was that there was an average of about forty or fifty a year.

Then, what was there incorrect in what we stated ? If we paid $60,000 and also the amount necessary to maintain the station, that being under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture, I do not think we misrepresented the facts when we said that we were paying dear for the immigration we get.

This is not a question of immigration. I am sure that when he thinks over the matter, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) will not insist upon the position he has taken. Would he wish to have small-pox brought into the country ?
We do uot want immigration to cost so dear as this.

If we have a quarantine, that quarantine must be equipped. Suppose that a ship comes with one or two thousand or even three thousand souls on board, you must have an equipment capable of handling that number. I have personal knowledge of cases when a thousand immigrants were located there. What would the country say and what would parliament say if a ship loaded with people, including some smitten with dangerous diseases, should come to our shores and no proper system of quarantine were provided ? In every part of the world there are quarantines. And I make bold to say that, under the late administration, there has been half a million dollars spent there. There are quarantines at St. John, at Halifax-there must be at every great port in the world.

What has that to do with the question under discussion ? We are talking about this quarantine station and about this proposed expense, not about what has been done elsewhere or in years gone by. The hon. minister finds it very convenient, when he gets into a hole, to say : You did the same. That is no argument. There is only one question to be considered, and that is whether this is not au enormous sum to spend, considering the public benefit derived. What information is it to me for the hon. gentleman to say that a great deal of money has been spent at Halifax and at other places ? Do we need to spend this amount of money at this particular station ?-that is the question. If it can be shown that the money can be spent in this way to the public advantage, we have nothing to say.

We require to equip our quarantines better than before, because we have a larger immigration than before. This is necessary to protect the health of the country. I think my hon. friends will admit on thinking it over, that their objections are not well taken.
Are these immigrants assisted immigrants ?

That lias nothing to do with the vote of $10,000 for quarantine. I do not know whether these immigrants are assisted or not. Tlie Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sif-ton), who will be in his place in a few days, will be able to answer as to that.

I think we are entitled to an answer to that point either from the hou. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) or from the minister in charge of immigration. Another thing we are entitled to know is whether any means are taken on the other side, whence these assisted immigrants come- immigrants who cost us so dear-to inspect them before they leave port.

Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) will see that it is not competent for me to answer his question. The quarantine for which I am asking money is the only one on thq St. Lawrence route during the summer months, and that quarantine I am equipping. When the immigration vote comes up, the hon. Minister of the Interior will be able to answer the hon. gentleman.

But, in order to know whether this is a proper amount to vote or not, we should have the information which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) asks for. How are we to know whether such a large sum of money ought to be spent at this station unless we know under what precautions assisted immigrants as well as others are taken on shipboard for Canada. If it is only for immigrants that this is desired
No, not only for immigrants.
It is mainly used for immigrants, I understand.
No, not principally.
I think the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) must be mistaken.
A good deal of the expenditure is necessary on account of immigrants, of course.
It is used, as I am informed-and I say it with all deference to the hon. minister-mainly for immigrants.

Quarantine work has no reference to immigrants or any other particular class of passengers arriving there. All passengers whether immigrants, or those travelling first-class, are quarantined exactly alike. As a matter of fact, I suppose, a larger number of those arriving by vessel arrive in the steerage than first or second-class. In that sense, it may be said that we are dealing Hon. Mr. TARTE.
principally with immigrants. But. if a thousand first-class passengers should arrive, this accommodation would be required just the same as for a thousand immigrants. The accommodation is required to be more extensive than is commonly used, because we must provide for contingencies. This was done by our predecessors, just as it is done by us. As to this vote and the votes of the last year or two for equipping our quarantine stations, I may say that our requirements have increased. We have been recommended by our medical authorities to provide more bathing accommodation for the people who are retained there. It is due to this that not only at Grosse Isle, but at other quarantine stations, the expenditure for equipment is greater than it used to be.

In cases of -this kind I am only a builder. The Department of Agriculture sends me a statement of the work to be done ; that is discussed with my chief architect and other officers, and I simply carry out the work for the Department of Agriculture. I trust my hon. friends will not persist in their objections. The season is about to open and this work has been begun. The quarantine must be equipped. It costs money, no doubt, but that is unavoidable. This vote is to complete the equipment of this important station, which is necessary to protect the health of the country.

If I remember rightly, the expenditure on this station in the past has been enorufous. It must represent a total of about $600,000 or $700,000. If I remember rightly, it is only a few years ago that nearly $120,000 was expended for fumigating purposes. There was a demand from the Department of Agriculture also for a wharf at Grosse Isle to accommodate vessels drawing twenty-eight or twenty-nine feet of water.
That has not been built.

So I understand. But a demand upon the government for such a wharf was made by the Department of Agriculture. The construction of that wharf would involve an expenditure of about $120,000. This question arose with the government at that day, and I suppose it lias been considered by the Minister of Public Works since, whether it would not have been better to abandon the station altogether and to take up another station which has been recommended as nearly as good, and where the expenditure would not be nearly as large. This seems to me an enormous sum of money for the small number of immigrants and passengers coming to this country who need to be accommodated there. It is not only on the buildings, but it is on the staff required at that particular place. I know that the duty of the Minister of Public Works is only ministerial, and that he has to carry out the request of

the Minister of Agriculture, who states that his officers have demanded this large expenditure there for the safety of the country and the prevention of epidemics. The expenditures have been very large in the past, and it behooves this House and the Minister of Public Works to look very carefully to see that no useless expenditure is made.

I think this will be the last expenditure we shall ask for. I may add that the expenditure we are incurring now has been decided on only after complete discussion between Hr. Montizambert, who is a very experienced officer, and my chief architect, and a good deal has been struck off the sum originally proposed.
What do the improvements consist of ?

There were no waterworks, and no sewerage. Indeed the quarantine station was in a very bad condition. The ventilation was bad, there were no water closets in the building. It was in an awful state when I was there myself two years ago.
Is it advisable to land immigrants at a place like that ?

I may say that the quarantine at Grosse Isle as well as that at St. John, when I saw them, were both in a very bad condition. It is because the buildings were in a dilapidated condition, and because we thought the quarantine station in such a condition constituted a danger to the country, that we felt obliged to ask for this large expenditure.

The Minister of Public Works excuses this very Ifirge expenditure by saying that he is only the builder. I think that is a very good excuse, and that the blame rests entirely on the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture told us a few minutes ago that in order to complete arrangements there it was necessary to provide bathing accommodation for these immigrants. Well, surely, a lesser sum than $10,000 would be amply sufficient to provide bathing accommodation for these gentlemen, unless their bathing is much more expensive than that which we resort to ourselves. I would like to know from the Minister of Public Works, upon whom such large demands are made by the Minister of Agriculture in favour of these immigrants, what is the work that remains to be done. Last year we had a discussion on a similar item and we had the same explanation-there were no waterworks, the buildings were in a dilapidated condition. We have the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that we must provide baths for the immigrants, and it is going to cost
$10,000. I think $5,000 would be amply sufficient, unless the Minister of Public Works gives us details now showing that it is not sufficient. I would like to know whether that work has been let by contract after tenders called for in the newspapers; if not, I am disposed to move for a reduction of that item.

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) overlooks the fact that this quarantine station is not only for immigrants but it is also designed to protect the whole country from disease coming in on the crews of ships. Last year a steamer was detained there forty days with over 300 immigrants on board. I believe the negro stoker on boaid the steamer had small-pox, and as a consequence 400 people were detained there over forty days. Several cases of that kind happen in the course of a year.
We do not refuse money that is necessary, but we want to know what it is used for.

The member for Jacques Cartier who spoke a moment ago ought to know better than to speak like that. What is the use of a man who is one of the leaders of the House saying that immigrants should not take expensive baths ? We know that. Our baths are not quarantine baths. But we all know what a quarantine is, the hon. gentleman knows what a quarantine is, and what is the use of his trying to throw dust in the eyes of the public by speeches such as that.
I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that is in order. I do not think it is in order to say that I am throwing dust in the eyes of the public.

Well, if the hon. gentleman had not done so, I certainly would not have referred to it. But I won't doi it again. But we all know that a quarantine station does not provide bathing for gentlemen, there is a vast difference. The expenditure last year was divided up among the following items: We have arranged for the installation of an electric light plant which is to cost $11,868. The grounds are very extensive grounds as my hon. friend knows. This is an island on which there are twenty-five buildings. We have built a new dwelling for employees, costing $8,000; water service, $2,260; repairs of building for police, painting, &c., $1,299; sidewalks, $1,275; dynamo building, $1,664; repairs to building for medical officers, $934; general repairs to buildings, $5,740. These are the largest items.

I should judge from the figures just presented by the minister that the sanitary condition could not havd been as bad as he pointed out a few minutes

ago. If I caught his figures correctly, _he only spent $2,000 for waterworks. There could not have been a very urgent case for sanitary improvement when only $2,000 or thereabouts were spent for waterworks.
I did not notice in the figures the minister read any expenditure for drainage purposes. Now, first-class sanitary arrangements would require a first-class water supply and first-class sewerage. If the sanitary condition was as bad as the minister says, a very small sum has been expended so far to improve that condition. We were discussing this matter a few nights ago, and if I may be permitted to refer to it, we were told then, under the immigration estimates, when we wanted to get some information, that we should wait until we discussed quarantine; while to-day when quarantine is up for discussion we are told that we cannot discuss immigration matters. I would like to ask the hon. minister, if it is in order to ask it now :	Would
it not be a better plan to have a more rigid inspection of immigrants before they leave Liverpool, or the point at which they embark to come to Canada ? I would also like some specific information from the hon. Minister of Public Works as to the amount that has been expended during the last two years for drainage purposes and also on account of a proper waterworks system.

1 would like to say, about the inspection of immigrants before they leave the point of departure, that even if that were undertaken, it would not relieve the department of the responsibility at the quarantine stations to any appreciable extent. Immigrants and other passengers would still have to be inspected at the quarantine port of debarkation and in case of disease occurring between one port or the other, immigrants or any other passengers would still have to be examined and would still have to have all this accommodation to receive them at the quarantine station, whether they had been inspected before leaving the ports in the old country or not. I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman and to the committee that the proposition, while a fair question of debate, in regard to immigrants, as far as quarantine is concerned, would not relieve the quarantine station of any responsibility, and I do not think of any expense. In regard to the demand for this vote, while I have not the details of the matter in the way that the hon. Minister of Public Works has, I would say that all these propositions were laid before the director general of public health, Dr. Montizambert, who has been for thirty-three years at the head of that service, practically, ever since the service was inaugurated and who has made far greater demands on my department and on the Public Works Department than have been complied with. There has been the demand Mr. CLARKE.
which the late Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) spoke of in regard to a wharf. There has been a demand for a much larger wharf at Grosse Isle, for one which would cost $75,000 or $100,000, but we have preferred to go on and try to do the work without that expenditure. The work is done just as effectively but not quite so conveniently as it would be with the wharf. But, we believe that it can be done effectively without that expenditure, and the hon. Minister of Public works has so far refrained from asking the House for that and some other expenditure of the same kind. In the case of an expenditure which involves the safety of the public health we would not have felt ourselves justified in refusing to take such precautions as the director general of public health deemed necessary for the safety of the public health.

May I ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if lie would give some more extended information as to the necessity of this building on which $8,000 was expended to provide accommodation for the employees on the island. Is there a larger number employed by the government now than formerly ? How were they housed previously to the erection of this building which has cost $8,000? I would like also to ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if the demands made by Dr. Montizambert for the improvement of the sanitary conditions at the station have been complied with ? We have pointed out to the lion. Minister of Public Works that in the estimates only $2,500 or $3,000 has been expended for the purposes of drainage and the improvement of the water system.
No, it is not that at all.

The items of this expenditure were before me while in consultation with the director general of public health some months ago, and they were then sent over to the Department of Public Works. I cannot carry the details of them in my mind, but there is no doubt that they are in the department.
I have just put my finger on the detail of the expenditure that was incurred last year. During the fiscal year of 1901 a system of waterworks and drainage was installed in the sick division.
What was the cost ?
I have not the amount of the cost. I am simply giving a summary of the work that has been done.
You gave us some figures a few moments ago.

Two tanks were housed, and a itew pump

building was erected in connection with this work.
What did that cost ?
Last year we had a vote of $30,000, out of which we have spent $21,000. There is no minister who can carry in his mind all the details of these expenditures.
You gave an expenditure $20,000, $8,000 for the building and $12,000 for other things.

Baths, basins, sinks and water closets were put into the hospitals and officers' dwellings. A new forge was built. The large hospital and the small pox hospital were reshingled; the first class detention building painted. Repairs were made to the telemeter, disinfection building and to the fire pot of the boiler for pump. Repairs were made to the wood, paint, plaster and other works of the different buildings. Some carpets and furniture were supplied. The steamer ' Challenger ' was overhauled and painted. Plans and specifications prepared by this department. The waterworks and drainage superintended by Mr. John Cowan, an old employee of the department, and the remainder of the work was supervised by Mr. Belaud, the contractor for waterworks and drainage were Messrs. O. Picard & Sons. We have speut on these works up to the first of February $28,000 out of the $30,000 that were placed in the estimates. We are asking for $10,000 additional to complete these works.

I do not think the lion. Minister of Agriculture has been quite fair to this committee, and I think the hon. Minister of Public Works has been placed in an unfortunate position by the statement made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture that this money was required to fulfil the requirements of the health authorities in respect to baths. We spent last year over $20,000 aud in that expenditure, which is found detailed at page V-68 of the Auditor General's Report, we find that everything that is required under the head mentioned by the hon. Minister of Agriculture was furnished during last year, and that is why I think this committee is entitled to know what the $10,000 additional is wanted for. I can understand that every detail of the expenditure cannot be kept in mind by the head of the department, but it seems to me that such an item as $20,000 for the instalment of waterworks should remain in the memory of the ordinary man for at least a few months. We had, last year, such expenditures as these: two Brussels rugs at $27, two Axminster rugs at $38, one mattrass, $18, one chamber set, $55, and in connection with the water accommodation we had sinks at $23 each aud bath tubs, 4 at $45 apiece, which seems a very large price to pay. Of course, I suppose, that the better class of
immigrants, or perhaps the employees, or the minister himself when he goes down to pay his annual visit required needle and shower baths, two of which were purchased at $145 ; flusher closets, 2 at $32 apiece and lavatory basins, 7 at $168. If we look over the expenditure we find that there is no ground whatever, as far as we can see, for granting an expenditure of $10,000 for the reason which has been given by the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I am ready to admit with the hon. Minister of Public Works that we must have a properly equipped quarantine station, but, when we see these extravagant expenditures, and are asked to vote $10,000, and are merely asking the head of the department to tell us what it is for, the department should have some information upon the subject.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) should know that these shower baths are used by the immigrants. They cost more than the ordinary shower baths. It seems to me that in this case the House will not lose sight of the fact that we are dealing with a large quarantine station and not with an ordinary private house. I have already explained that out of the $30,000 voted last year we have spent $28,048.57 for water works, for drainage for baths, for new pumps for basins and sinks and water closets in the hospital and officers quarters. The large small-pox hospital has been re-shingled. I made a mistake in giving the details. What I read from my notes was work that was to be done and not work that had been done. We made a contract for electric lighting amounting to $11,868, and we have paid to the contractors $5,500, leaving a balance due of $6,363. That will be taken out of the vote of $10,000. In addition to that there is $1,000 for electric light fittings not included in the contract. There is for water service $2,160 and for repairs $1,299. What I read first was a list of works which had been asked for and practically granted but for which we had no money.

I understood from the minister that the quarantine station was in a very unsanitary condition and that there was not sufficient drainage. The minister states that there is $2,160 for water service and for electric light $12,868. What I want to know is how much will be spent in drainage to put the buildings in a sanitary condition
I understand that about $4,000 has been spent for drainage, and that we are doing work now that will cost $3,160.
Where are the figures for that ?
The chief architect has given this information to me. These sums have been paid out of the vote of $30,000 of last year.
How much did the director general ask for these sanitary improvements ?
I do not know how much he asked for.
The director general asks that certain sanitary improvements should be made, and it is left to the Public Works Department to say what they will cost.
And the sanitary improvements asked for by the director general have been made ?

Most of them have been made but there is a certain amount still necessary to finish the whole plan of improvement. The amount which is now asked for is to pay for the work which was asked by the director general of public health. The vote taken last year did not quite meet the requirements, and we have to have a supplementary vote this year to cover the balance. That work is not absolutely finished although it is very nearly finished, and when it is finished I believe the station will be in a thoroughly good sanitary state.
Had the minister no idea of the cost that would be entailed on the public by carrying out the demands made by the director general of public health ?
These estimates were made by the Public Works Department.
' Was there no estimate made, by the Department of Agriculture ?
We do not undertake to make estimates.
And the Department of Agriculture had no idea of what expenditure would be entailed by the improvements asked for ?
We discuss that with the Public Works Department and we leave it to that department to make the estimates.
We have not yet been able to get the information that we have asked for.
I think I gave all the information that was asked for, but I will give all that is in my possession. We spent $28,048.57 up to the first of February out of the $30,000 which was voted last year.
How much for drainage ?

$4,000. We owe to the contractor for electric light, $0,668 ; we require electric light fittings to the amount of $1,000 ; to complete our water service we require. $2,360; and for repairs, painting, drains. &c.,

we require $1,190. Other demands have been made upon us, but for these I am not asking for money. I made a mistake is saying that part of this $10,000 was to erect an $8,000 building. The $10,000 is to be employed for the objects which I have mentioned.
L'Assomption public building, $5,000.
Has the site been chosen for this building ?

We have bought a site, for which we have paid $1,150.
ill-. MONK. Who from ?

From a gentleman of the name of Vital Racette. I do not propose to ask for an expensive building. 1 do not expect to expend more than $5,000, including fittings and all. L'Assomption parish contains a large population, and I may say that I have some love for the place.
What is the population ?

Two thousand six hundred.
Mi-. MONK. Is the work given out ?
No, the plans are not yet made. We have simply bought the site.
I suppose the work will be done by tender publicly called ?
Oh, certainly.

I have no objection to a public building being erected at L'Assnmption, but I reiterate what was first mentioned here by the hon. member for Bothwell, that 1 thiqk we should know what are the general principles-the minister objects to the term fixed rule-which govern the government in the distribution of public buildings throughout our province. I am glad to see a public building proposed for L'Assomption, which is an important place; but there are other places which I think have equal claims. I could mention a place in my own constituency. Take Cote St. Paul, which has a large manufacturing population, which is situated on the Lachine canal, and which is just as important as this place. Then, there are very important factories situated in the neighbourhood of Verdun, which is a growing locality. I believe there is a public building at Laprairie, but there is noue at Longueuil, nor at Chambly, both of which are important places. I think we are entitled to know what are the conditions we should fulfil in order to lay our claim before the minister.

I think the plea which the hon. gentleman has made for St. Laurent might well guide


me in this case. St. Laurent is an important place; it has a college. L'Assomption also has a college, one of the largest in the province of Quebec; it has eighty stores, six hotels, a telegraph office and two convents, and it is a shire town. I cannot give public buildings to all the towns which should perhaps have them; but the expediency of not spending too much money cannot be lost sight of. L'Assomption is an old village, it has not received anything in the past, and we thought we might vote a small sum for a public building there. I would like very much indeed to give public buildings to other towns as deserving, but their time will come.
What was the revenue from that place last year ?
The total revenue from the post office was $910. The money orders issued were $4,881.
Would it not be very much cheaper for the governtnent to rent a building which is already constructed, instead of putting a large amount of money in a new building ?

There are many places where we rent buildings; but I may say that there are not merely dozens, but hundreds of demands for public buildings in my department. When I hear speeches in the House against public buildings, I would like some of my friends to persuade their own people not to ask for buildings. It is very well to preach economy here, but our pigeon holes are full of petitions asking for public buildings; and when I have plans prepared, I would like to see around me economical people, such as I see here, advising me not to have expensive buildings. The life is almost taken out of me sometimes because I decline to erect expensive buildings. I have to face a good deal of pressure on account of the numerous demands made upon me, and because people want fine buildings. They say, we are erecting fine houses for ourselves and fine stores, and you want to pursue a cheese-paring policy in regard to public buildings.

Perhaps some of the hon. gentleman's difficulty arises from a circular which the hon. gentleman's colleague the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) sent out in the spring of 1900, calling on his friends to make suggestions for the construction of public buildings ; and I have no doubt that the hon. minister has reprimanded his colleague for taking that step in his absence, because at that time the hon. gentleman was in raids. Of course, if he had been here it would not have been done. That may to some extent account for the difficulty which the hon. gentleman has iu denying the demands so frequently made upon him now.
I think it is a pity that the Minister of Public Works puts an improper

construction on what I said. I am not opposed to public buildings, but I want to know what is the proper path by which we can reach the heart of the Minister of Public Works when we want* a public building. This circular, which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has alluded to, never reached me. I never got one, although two or three public buildings are required iu my constituency. If the Minister of Public Works would only tell us that there are absolutely necessary conditions precedent, without which he cannot entertain a demand for a public building, we will know where we are. But as a man of business, he will admit we ought to know what are the principles that guide him.

I frankly admit that if I had been here I would not have felt under any necessity to advertise that I wanted applications for public buildings. My hon. colleague, as a prudent man, wanted to know the needs of the country, but if he had been a little longer in the Department of Public Works and had read as much of the correspondence as I have, he would have known the needs of the country quite well enough not to require any more knowledge. I can assure my hon. friend that I have not a bad heart, and if he will approach me in one of his good moments, and when I am not in a bad humour, we might agree.

The hon. gentleman takes the case of Marysville as the standard by which he intends going on granting public buildings. If that be the case, I think he had better make some further inquiries, and he will find that he is not living up to that standard. Take my own county, which is perhaps a fair average of the counties of this Dominion. It has four towns, and I will give the hon. gentleman the gross postal revenue in each, which ought to be a fair indication of the business done and the necessity for a public building. In the town of Marysville the hon. gentleman tells us that the gross postal revenue, according to the last returns, is $1,398. Compare that with the four towns in my own county. The town of Wallaceburg, with a population of 2,700, has a gross revenue of $3,207, as against $1,398 in the town of Marysville. The town of Dresden, with a population of 1,000, has a gross revenue of $1,948. And the town of Thamesville, with some 900 of population, has a gross revenue of $1,080. Then take the little town of Botliwell, with about 800 inhabitants, its gross revenue is $1,078, as against $1,398 in Marysville. And I venture to say the hon. gentleman would not dream of erecting a public building in any one of these three places.
Let me go a little further and take the money orders issued and see how Marysville compares with the towns I have meu-tioned. In Marysville the number of money I orders issued was 50, and the gross stun in-

volved only $748. But in Wallaceburg, which has been asking for a post office since many years, the number of money orders issued is 1,204, and the gross sum involved $14,523. Take Dresden, there were 852 money orders issued as against 50 in Marysville, and the gross sum involved was $13,411. Then in Tliamesville, 370 money orders were issued and the sum involved $5,S70 ; and finally in Bothwell, which has only 800 inhabitants, there were 1,250 post office orders issued, and the gross sum involved was $14,909.
Now, let us take the number of orders paid. In Marysville the number was only G4 as against 653 in Wallaceburg, 552 in Dresden, 286 in Thamesville, and 352 in Bothwell. Take the gross sum involved in each :
Marysville	$ 555
Wallaceburg,	 9,431
Dresden,	 7,256
Thamesville	 3,816
Bothwell	 4,444
If these returns indicate anything they certainly indicate that the hon. gentleman lias chosen one of the least deserving places in this Dominion in which to erect a public building. I know of no more vicious case than this one to show the utter want of regard for the public needs and the public weal which dictates the hon. gentleman's policy. The sole principle which guides him is party necessity. Wherever there is an election to be gained, wherever it suits the purposes of the government, he is quite ready to put up a public building, regardless entirely of the needs of the public or the requirements of the locality.

There are certain ridings which are unlucky, and the riding represented by my hon. friend is one of them. He has explained that in his riding there are four towns which ought to have had public buildings long ago. Well, that riding was represented in parliament by a Liberal, the Hon. David Mills, for many years, and no public buildings were then allotted to it. The chances of war have given us my hon. friend, but he is on the wrong side.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent me. I was not saying whether there should be public buildings there or not, but I was pointing out that there should be some broader ground of public policy in determining what places were entitled to public buildings than what the hon. gentleman has given us.

My hon. friend gave us the names of four towns, each of which, in his opinion, is better entitled to a public building than the town of Marysville. Well, I was simply reminding him that the riding of Bothwell was for many years represented with great Mr. CLANCY.
ability by one of our friends, the Horn David Mills. During those years my hon-friends opposite were on these government benches, and yet it never occurred to them that any one of these four towns was worthy of a public building. I do not see, therefore, how they can find fault with us. We have given ridings represented by opponents public buildings. I do not say-because I am not in the habit of saying what I do not believe to be true- that the representative of a riding has no influence at all; that would be a foolish thing to say. Now that hon. gentlemen on the other side have supplied all their ridings with public buildings, they must not be surprised, if we, on coming into power, pay some attention to ours. That is the position I take without hesitation. Let us be fair to our hon. friends on the other side, but-we should be great fools if we did not think of ourselves. If hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side, they would say exactly what I say now. Of course, we must not squander public money on useless buildings-wo all agree to that. I do not object to being criticised ; I do not object to the brake of the opposition being put upon any minister-far from it. But there is reason in all things. The Liberal party has been long in opposition, and ridings that have been for so long neglected by the government have rights that I, for one, will endeavour not to forget. As to the item of Marysville. I would remind my hon. friends opposite that their reproaches come not merely with little grace, but with no grace whatever. I found a vote for this work in the estimates when I took office, a vote put there by the late Minister of Finance-and I have simply carried it out.
I understood that the policy of the late government was to distribute these expenditures for public buildings upon a principle based upon the revenue and population of the town.
Not much.

Perhaps I could give these hon. gentlemen quotations from their own speeches on that point. Here is the policy as it was explained by the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). This is from the debate on the Richmond post office.
What year was it 7

Of course, hon. gentlemen opposite will understand that they do not occupy the same position now as they did then. This was the year 1894. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) said :
I know that the hon. ministers and members on that sidethat is the conservative side

Voted that public money should be expended upon these buildings on some principle based

on the revenue at the points where these buildings are being constructed and the population to be served.
Then another distinguished gentleman on that side (Mr. Charlton) said :
In a little place like Richmond, with a moderate revenue it strikes me the economical plan would be to rent quarters. And the accommodation might be had at a cost of $200 a year.
The policy of the Conservative party as described by the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries is in marked contrast to the policy of the present administration, who say that it depends upon what the county does in sending a representative to support the government, how it shall De considered in the distribution of money in the construction of public buildings.

Unfortunately, in that, as in a good many other cases, the practice was vastly different from the precept avowed.
I have the honour to represent one of the richest, oldest and most populous constituencies in Ontario, and my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) represents another. Ingersoll and Woodstock, the chief places of these two very large and wealthy constituencies, remained for very nearly forty years without a public building of any kind, sort or description, while, almost within sight of us, was the village of Cayuga, with 150 families, which was thought worthy of a public building. That was a very fair sample of the way government favours were distributed during the period which the Conservatives were in office.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The argument of the hon. Minister of Public Works, which was hailed with such delight by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock), and the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), amounts simply to this-and it is well that we should understand it-the constituency represented by my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), we will say, was not treated fairly by the late Conservative government because it was represented by an opponent of theirs, Hon. David Mills, and so went without public buildings in places that were much more deserving than is Marysville ; and now, because that constituency happens to be represented by a gentleman who is opposed to the present government, that injustice must be continued.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: That is what the hon. gentleman's argument amounts to. He says that the Conservative party treated that constituency unfairly in the past, because it was represented by an opponent of theirs. Then the Minister of Public Works very frankly tells us in this nousewhat has been said by himself and his colleagues on many a public platform-that the representation of a constituency is not without its effect in the distribution of public moneys. The public moneys, under this administration, are not to be distributed according to the public requirements, but according to the political complexion of the gentlemen who represent the constituencies -at least, that is to be taken into consideration. Now, if there is one principle which is more unworthy of the government than another, or more unworthy of the Minister of Public Works, it is that which he defends to-day, and which the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has defended.
I simply called attention to the discrepancy between Conservative practice and Conservative precedent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), in my humble opinion, would have done better to have stood up and told his colleagues that when this party of purity came into power public moneys were to be distributed according to the needs of the country and not according to the political complexion of the representatives of the constituencies. From the record in the past of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce we might expect some repudiation of the views expressed by his colleagues jo-day. But, instead, he merely throws a taunt at this side of the House with regard to what was done by Conservative administrations in the past. The conduct of Conservative administrations is not the question here. The question is, what is right and best to do to-day ; and, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce has no better ground for defending the present administration than to say that some such thing was done unjustly in the past, it seems to me, with all deference to the hon. gentleman, that it would be better for his own reputation for him to keep his seat. I say again that the argument of the Minister of Public Works is a most vicious argument. Let us concede even, for the purpose of this argument, that the Conservative government did wrong in the past. What has that to do with the question of what is right and best at the present time. Because previous governments did wrong, does that fact of itself justify the present government in following their example ? I venture to say that, whatever has been done in the past with regard to the distribution of public money, the standard in the future should be that the money expended in this country for public works should be expended on some broad and systematic policy according to the needs of the constituency, and absolutely apart from the question as to whether a constituency happens to be represented by a supporter of the government or by a gentleman on this side of the House.

I will say this to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that, for a period of nearly thirty years, the Liberal party was treated, systematically and deliberately, by the predecessors of the hon. gentleman with the grossest injustice. And one of the first duties that fell upon us when we assumed office was to see that justice was done to our supporters and to those constituencies which had been deprived of their rights for a great many years. When I gave the illustration of the counties of South Oxford and North Oxford, I gave those because they were extremely notable illustrations of the systematic injustice that had been dealt out to Liberal constituencies for no worse crime than returning Liberal supporters. Now I am glad to see the hon. gentleman's education is beginning. I daresay after they have spent eighteen years in opposition, as they are very likely to do, they will come to something like a glimmering understanding of the principles on which governments ought, in an ideal fashion, to be conducted. I do not disapprove of the statement he makes that it is desirable that regard should be had in all these cases to the amount of the population, to the amount of the revenue, and to various other things which we have often pointed out as having necessarily and properly a large influence on such questions as the erection of public buildings. But I have to tell the hon. gentleman that, as I have said just now, it is the duty of a party which has been long in opposition, when they get into office, to rectify the injustices which were deliberately inflicted by the party in power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not know that the hon. gentleman has improved very much upon his predecessors. According to him, the first duty of a party coming to power, after being out of power for eighteen years, is, not to conduct the government in the best interests of the country-
I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
But he said it by implication-but to look after thp interests of the party that had been in opposition. Now this is the gentleman, if I mistake not, who preached political purity and high standards of government for eighteen years. Now we understand that his ideal is this, that when his party gets into power the first thing to be looked after is, not these high standards about which he told us so much during eighteen years, but the interests of the Liberal party. Well, he has looked after them pretty well in some respects, I believe. But still possibly principles of that kind, even if they are professed by hon. gentlemen on the other side, had better not, for the credit of the country, be too loudly proclaimed in this Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
House. I think it would be better to put on some semblance of political decency with regard to this matter, and not to say in this House that because a constituency has been represented by a Liberal in the' past and therefore has not received justice, it shall, because it happens to be represented by a Conservative now, receive, not the justice which it should receive, but the continued injustice which it has received in the past, and that for no better reason than that it happens to be represented by a gentleman on this side of the House. That is the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
It is not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am glad I have been able to provoke so vigorous a disclaimer from that hon. gentleman, and I trust that when he thinks the matter over a little more calmly he will come to the conclusion that it is not wise in this House to lay down the doctrine of party spoils in so open and flagraut a manner as he has just presented it to the House to-day.
Politics are indeed a very fine game.
It is a bluff game.

Yes, we have a proof of it just now. For over twenty-five years I have seen the game from the press gallery of this Plouse, and history repeats itself. When the Conservative party was on this side of the House the Liberals said a great many things that the Conservative opposition are saying now. Now, if my hon. friends opposite will excuse me for saying it, they do not always feel very comfortable at the present time. They are afraid of the war, and after the speeches that my hon. friends opposite are delivering to-day, they will not feel any more comfortable in the event of their resuming office in the future. As I say, politics is a fine game, it is an amusing game. My hon. friend has taught me a lesson, he has invited me to decency. Well, I have a good deal of respect for him, but I have always tried to have some respect for myself; and I am quite sure that in what I have already stated to the House, and which will be read by the country, I have not been transgressing decency. I have said this much, and I say it again, that the representatives of the party in power have naturally more influence with the government than the representatives of the party opposed to the government. That is very clear, and what is the use of denying it V I do not make any personal allusion, but what is the use of resorting to hypocrisy V People do not take any stock in that now, it is too late in the day. The government in power is very largely guided

by the advice of its own political friends, because those political friends represent public opinion for the time being. But that does not mean that the public interest must be ignored because that interest happens to be located in a riding represented by a member of the opposition. Nobody has intimated anything of the kind. There are to-day very large public works going on in ridings represented by supporters of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. We have not been hard towards members of the opposition. In point of fact we have been reproached many times by our political friends with being too kind to Conservatives. Beveral times I have been accused myself of being an old Tory because I did not do what some of my Liberal friends wished me to do, because I did not give them enough. Responsible government is the government of the people by the representatives of the people, by the majority of the people. Our friends opposite must not be offended if we invite them in the most kindly way to take their medicine patiently. They are in opposition, they are doing a useful duty in criticising us, they are doing it well; but they must not forget that the party which is in office to-day represents a majority of the people in the country, and that part of the country represented by the majority has to be attended to.

There is just one interesting observation of the hou. gentleman which I would like you, Mr. Chairman, to note. He states that criticisms of this kind were very frequently heard some years ago on this side of the House from gentlemen who now sit on the government side of the House; and then he tells us in the same breath that he does not like hypocrisy. I do not know what the hon. gentleman had in his own mind when he made that statement to the House. We are not putting forward these criticisms without meaning them-if that is what the hon. gentleman desires to suggest. We are putting forward in all earnestness the principle that the public money of this country should be distributed according to the public needs of the country. I do not know whether my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works agrees with that; apparently he qualifies it by saying that the principle must be modified by the question as to whether the member representing the particular constituency supports the government or not. With regard to that principle we entirely disagree. I will not say anything further about it except to state that so far as I am concerned I do not believe that is good policy for the country. It is a policy which was not supported by hon. gentlemen in opposition, but it does apparently have some weight with them now since they have acquired the responsibility of power.

I think we are indebted to the Minister of Mr. SPROULE.
! Public Works for several confessions. Not long ago he took the public into his con-iidence, in Montreal, I think it was, when he told them that the cabinet was largely engaged in fighting each other like blazes. To-day he announces that the supporters of this government, and this government themselves, adhere to the doctrine that to the victors belong the spoils. I suppose most of their time is taken up, since they have no legislation for us to consider at this session, in fighting among themselves for a share of the spoils.
I have only one thing to say, I shall never make any more after dinner speeches.

So far as I can see there is absolutely no public interest to be served in this vote. If there ever was a vote purely and simply meant to serve a local interest, a political interest, it is such a vote as this, and such votes as we have had on several of these items this afternoon. What public interest is there to be served bv an expenditure of $5,000, $10,000, $15,000, or $20,000 of public money in a village on a post office where the whole revenue is under $1,000 ? Can it be justified in any way except as a pure and simple expenditure of public money for party purposes ? There cannot be any more glaring deviation of public money from the right channel than in such a vote as this. It was rather refreshing to have from the various members of the government, as they one after another got up to justify this vote, the admission that when they were in opposition and objected to such votes, they were ideal statesmen. They never thought for a moment of putting into practice their ideals when they came into power. I do not think, in the whole list of estimates, there are better subjects for criticism than these items of expenditure of large sums of money in small places where they are not required and where they can only be made because of some local political influence being brought to bear.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if the department is in the habit of preparing plans and specifications for public buildings when they are undertaken ?
We generally prepare the plans, but on some occasions when we are busy we employ outside help.

There is another important matter in connection with the construction of public buildings that has not been discussed to-day. While I do not differ with the government as to their satisfying their friends by erecting public buildings, it seems to me that when the department prepares plans and specifications, it should also arrive at some conclusion as to the time it should take to construct a public building.
<667

We have a large number of public buildings constructed in this country from time to time, and there is no stated rate of pay for the architects or clerks of works employed by the Department of Public Works, because I find in the Auditor General's Report and referring to Vancouver, that the architect and clerk of works get $120 per month. I find that in Woodstock the architect receives $100 a month; I find that in Nelson the pay is $7 a day, and I find that in Toronto as high as 71 per cent, 7 per cent, 31 per cent, 1 per cent, and large lump sums are paid to an architect for superintending public works.
