If the government does not pay some attention as to the time that it requires to erect a public building, it will be paying all over the country, in every town, city and village, in which it constructs a public building, large sums of money to these architects for a useless waste of time in superintending these public works. Therefore it is not in the public interest that these men should be continued for these long periods. Take the Auditor General's Report to-day, and you will find, under the heading of ' Public Buildings,' from the 1st of July to the 30th of June in the following year, twelve months' pay for an architect for superintending a public building that ought to be constructed in at least six mouths' time. These items, taken altogether, are very important, if the hon. gentleman desires to satisfy his friends by erecting public buildings. For instance, in Wallaceburg, for a building that may cost $8,000 or $10,000, an architect is paid $2,000 for superintending it. Perhaps this practice has been abused under the Conservative regime and if it has it is certainly being abused under the present administration, because it is not a proper thing to do.
Levis cattle quarantine station-renewals, improvements, repairs, etc., $3,000.
Plow much was expended last year ?
Five thousand dollars last year.
What is it for ?
No special work, but just for general repairs.
Are these expenditures being made on the advice of somebody ?
Yes, always on the advice of the Department of Agriculture. In this case, as in all other cases, I am simply the builder. Demands are made upon me.
I understood the hon. minister to say that he spent $5,000 last year.
Yes.
And that he proposes to spend $5,000 this year ?
No, $3,000 this year.
That would buy all the buildings on the place.
These buildings were erected twenty years ago and they require a good deal of repairing.
Why do you require $8,000 to repair buildings not worth $2,000 ?
They were built a long time ago, and they are always requiring repairs.
What are they for-cattle ?
Yes.
To what extent do we import cattle ?

The list that has been sent to us of the work that is to be done this year includes two new stables, $1,250; rebuilding fences, $1,793; repairing roads, $1,000; superintendent's office, $308; other employees' residence, repairs, $275; repairing old stable, $60; sidewalks, $2S7; small repairs, $266. The whole amount that we were asked for was $5,500, but we have cut it down to the amount I have just asked for now.
What are the roads on which it is proposed to spend $1,000 ?
They are roads communicating between the different buildings. I have been there often. There are at least ten or twelve acres of property.
It is for thoroughbred stock that is imported ?

As a matter of fact, there is very little stock imported except thoroughbred stock, but all stock arriving has to be quarantined for ninety days, and the accommodation is required for this stock. There has to be a yard for each particular lot of cattle with a space between, so that the animals in one yard cannot come in contact with, or even within easy reach of the animals in the adjoining yard. This fencing has been in very bad order, and last year a report came that it was necessary to reifiace it. The buildings which were erected twenty years ago have had very little done on them for many years, and were in such a very bad state that the importers were complaining.
What quantity of stock was imported last year ?
Speaking from memory, about 1,500 or 1,000 head of cattle, sheep and swine.
Were they all imported from Great Britain ?
One lot I think came from France, but all the rest came from Great Britain.
This appears to be an enormous sum to replace fencing on ten or twelve acres of ground.
I will bring over the details to the hon. gentleman and he can see for himself what the cost is.
I do not see how you can spend all that money for fencing a plot of twelve acres.

Speaking from memory there are forty acres in the lot, so that it is erroneous to say that it contains only twelve acres. The buildings have to be placed at some distance apart and have all to be fenced around. It is a rough piece of ground and we have to grade roads so that provender can be carried to the cattle. For a long time there were no roads and the inconvenience was found to be such that the importers requested that we should make these improvements.
You would appear, by these estimates, to intend to build sidewalks on the streets of the town.

It is not on the streets of the town. There is some planking necessary around the grounds to enable the attendants to go dry shod from one building to another, and that is called a side walk.
L6vis public building, $5,000.
Ml1. MONK. Is this work under contract ?
No. No site.has been purchased and nothing has been done.
Why are we asked to vote the money then ?
Because I expect to go along now.
Has the minister made choice of any site ?

No. There are some changes to be made by tlie Railway Department and I was in expectation of being able to secure the old freight shed for a site. No choice has been made yet, and I do not know whether I will be able to get the freight shed site as I have not been able to confer lately with my colleague who has been away practically for the last three months.
Of course the contract will be given by public tender when the building comes to be erected.

Certainly.
Montreal examining warehouse, $15,000.
What is this for ?

That building will have to be changed altogether inside, and we are adding another story to it. It is too dark and cannot accommodate the trade which is increasing every day. I went there a month ago with one of the architects and Mr. Miles, the President of the Montreal Board of Trade. My officers believe they can carry out the work for $30,000. The estimate is as follows Addition to building, $6,000 ; altering main building inside, $12,000 ; fittings, $4,000 ; light, $500 ; furniture, $1,000 ; heating, $1,000 ; contingencies, $500. Although I am not an architect I am about sure that the addition will cost a little more than $6,000.
I would like to have the assurance of the minister that these repairs, if absolutely necessary, will be carried on by contract.
The work cannot be carried on that way.

Why not ? There is very keen competition in Montreal among builders and I really think we are not getting the worth of our money in the repairs we have been executing on public buildings in Montreal during the last four or five years. I feel convinced that if the minister will make specifications of what repairs are necessary, and will invite tenders fairly and publicly he will effect a considerable economy. Why should not the government do that ? Private individuals and companies do that. We have architects in Montreal-and the minister has some of them at his disposal in his department-who are continually making repairs under such a system as that. We will vote the money at once if the minister gives us the assurance that there will be specifications deposited where contractors can see them and tenders invited fairly and publicly.

In the case of work like this no railway company, or no other company would think for one moment of calling for public tenders. Neither would a private person do it. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) himself owns houses and when be has repairs to make he does not call for tenders. When you start out on work like this you never know what you will have to do. There is not a man in this House who owns property who will call for

tenders for such repairs. I have tried that system in repairing wharfs and breakwaters, and I have always found myself in deep water because it is impossible to know before hand the extent of the repairs.
You are adding a story to that building.
That is only a small part of the work. The Canadian Pacific Railway is improving their, station in Montreal and there was no tender asked for.
I beg your pardon, it was done by tender and contract.
No.
Yes, I know the contractors.

The material may be obtained by contract, but the work is done by day's labour. In this case I believe that I will spend less money if I do the work by day's labour. I cannot understand the argument that has been made often in this department that the government cannot carry on work by day's labour, just the same as contractors can. I decline to admit that because experience has proven that it is not true. I say more : It does not give him any pleasure to carry out work's by day's labour; it gives him trouble. But I say that the system of the public tenders as carried out in this country is a bad system. If tenders were asked from a picked list of contractors as is done in Germany and in France it would be well and good; but when everybody who can find a deposit is allowed to send in a tender as is the case here, that is the worst possible system. 1 say, after five years of experience In the department, that the poorer the contractor is the lower tender will he send in. He does not know his business; he will try to buy his matei'ial on credit. Several important works are to-day delayed because they are in the hands of men who should not have been allowed to tender. What is the position of the minister when an incapable or unworthy contractor does not carry on the work properly V If I take the work from him, I have to ask for new tenders, which means two or three months of delay. The system of public tenders which we have is a bad one, and every time we have repairs to be made, I do not hesitate to say to the House on my responsibility that it should be done by day's labour. Of course, large works, like the Halifax public building, for instance, I would not wish to do by day's labour.
If the principle is a sound one, why not 7
I do not see why not. I have to educate the public and parliament first-that is the

whole trouble. I do not hesitate to say that the work which we are carrying on at Sorel, building cars and dredges, is better carried out than it would be if it. were done by contract. The government has no interest except to do the work well. The contractor expects to realize a profit of 20 per cent, because he has to buy his plant, Ac., but when a government has the plant, it can put into the work the profits which any contractor would wash to make.

I am very sorry to hear the lion. Minister of Public Works enunciate that doctrine, because 1 believe that in the city of Montreal repairs amounting to $lo,-000, and consisting principally of putting an additional story on the examining warehouse, ought to be given out by public tender. The law requires it, and m the city of Montreal no institution nor individual would think of carrying on such works without inviting public tenders. The hon. gentleman has mentioned the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is well known that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have accredited contractors who sometimes undertake alterations without submitting the price; but they are really clerks of works, and they usually exact contracts from those under them. The hon. gentleman has referred to the extension of the Windsor Station in Montreal. I repeat that in that case there were large contracts for plumbing and heating, given to Lessard & Harris by tender.
1 do the same thing. While carrying out the work by day's labour, I ask for tenders for plumbing or steam fitting.

If the hon. gentleman will make specifications for these repairs and invite public tenders, he will find that he can get the work done by able and responsible contractors for half the cost at which it will be done by day's labour or by calling on two or three friends of the government for prices. Now, we spend about $60,000 a year on repairs in Montreal, and I venture to say that there is no city in the Dominion of Canada where the service of the government are so badly accommodated as in Montreal. If we spend so large an amount annually on repairs and improvements in Montreal, we ought surely to be able to get something better than We have at present. If I had the time, I could show, by reference to the public accounts of last year, that money could have been saved if the minister had followed the plan which is followed by everybody else in Montreal, of asking for public tenders. I regret that the minister evidently intends dealing with these repairs, for which he asks $15,000, without the condition of calling for public tenders. If he would attach that condition to the vote, I would be ready to concede it at once, because 1 know that the improvements are necessary.

I am dealing with the repairs in Montreal in the same way as my predecessors have done, and they are under the charge of the same officers. Mr. Desjardins is an old officer whom I left in office, although not a political friend of mine. He was appointed by my predecessor Mr. Ouimet, but I left him in office, because I believed he was an honest man, and I believe so still.
You are not to be bound by everything that was done by the previous government.

I am fully responsible for what I am doing; but I say that the repairs are being carried out on the same system that prevailed in the past, and it is the only system on which they can be carried out. We have in Montreal the examining warehouse, the custom-house, the inland revenue office and the post office. Now, how could you possibly ask for tenders for every small work costing $50 or less-for a little painting or to repair something that has got out of order ? It is practically impossible to find out in advance all the repairs that may become necessary. We are nearly all owners of houses, and there is not a man here who does not spend a large amount of money on his houses. Can he tell to-day how much money he will have to spend during the coming year ? , He cannot. My hon. friend is altogether unfair to the officers in charge of the work in Montreal. I follow them closely, and I say without hesitation that they carry out the work cheaply and well. I think my hon. friend is right when he says that the post office is not in good shape. The reason is, if I may say so, that there has been, in the past, a division of power. The Postmaster General's Department has done part of the cleaning and my department has done the rest. That has caused a very bad state of affairs-I grant that. We have arranged to put a stop to that. I have provided for a lodging upstairs, for a caretaker for the building. In future, I think we shall have better results, while expending less money. '

Will the hon. minister please say what is the result, usually, of carrying out these public works by day labour ? Does he find that the estimates are exceeded or is the work done within the estimates made by his officers ?

At times, the estimates are exceeded. That is the case, for instance, in the addition made to this building. Any one who knows anything about repairs knows how that may easily be. When you start, you think the structure is good, but may find you are mistaken. In this case the architect was obliged to go to a depth of fifteen feet for his foundation. He could not have foreseen 22
that-nobody could. In cases like that, it is impossible to carry out the system of tender and contract. As a rule, the estimates are found to be all right.

In the specific case of the post office at Montreal, I understand that there was a division of authority and that the results were not good-which is quite likely. But, in that case, what was the difficulty ?
The Minister of public works.
There was no difficulty. I understood my hon. friend to complain that the Montreal post office was not kept clean. That was true. I explained how that was and that I had provided lodging for a caretaker who would have responsibility for the whole building.

The expenditure of $10,000 or $15,000 in the Montreal post office without the formality of calling for tenders is a very trifling matter compared with the startling announcement that the minister has made within the last few minutes. Practically he has told us that, from this out, he intends to confine himself to the principle of getting tenders from his friends without the formality of public competition. The Department of Marine and Fisheries introduced that method under the late minister to a certain extent, and perhaps it is to be the rule now in the other departments of the government. Last session, I called the attention of the House to the fact that the Minister of Public Works was spending vast sums of money at Sorel without calling for tenders. I am not going to say that the work done at Sorel costs more or costs less than it would have cost under public tender and contract. But I am surprised that some hon. gentleman on the other side has not stood up and told the hon. minister that he must call a halt on this line of procedure. What is the minister doing at Sorel according to the last Auditor General's Report ? It will be news to some hon. members of the House, and perhaps to some hon. members of the government, that, at this place, the Minister of Public Works employs an army of men, the expenditure for whose work runs not merely into the thousands but into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Have we come to this pass, that the Minister of Public Works can employ hordes of men, building and repairing boats as he pleases-for there is no explanation up to this time as to what has actually been done ? According to the last Auditor General's Report the minister spent about $125,000 in this way. Last year I brought to the attention of the House the case of the construction of a tug at a cost of about twice what was really necessary. The machinery was . on the upper lakes, having been taken out of the old hull. A new hull was built at Sorel and was then towed around to the upper lakes. The cost would have been fifty per cent less



if the hull had been built at Midland and the machinery placed in it there. Here at page V-19 of the Auditor General's Report, we have some account of the expenditure at Sorel, amounting to this enormous sum of about $125,000-and it is an enormous sum to be expended at the sweet will of the Minister of Public Works. What is the procedure at Sorel ? I will be bound to say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bruneau) who represents Richelieu, in which riding I understand Sorel to be, simply turns on his party friends in season and out of season. To do what ? To work at whatever work can be provided. The principle of competition is set at defiance. Yet, not an hon. gentleman on the other side rises to call the minister to account. That hon. gentleman, this afternoon, has made the startling announcement that he does not intend to be held to the system of tender and contract in a matter involving the expenditure of $15,000 or $20,000. Then what is the hon. minister going to do with the case of the French River canal ?

It will be all open.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

We heard before recess from the Minister of Public Works, who is nothing if not candid, the frank and exultant avowal that he had initiated a new system of dispensing with calling for tenders for government contracts, and had thus secured control of an amount of patronage undreamed of by his predecessors. From his point of view the hon. minister is rather to be congratulated on the success of his experiment. During the past four or five years in which he has been at the head of the Public Works Department he has taken the bull by the horns, and certainly can have no cause of complaint of the result. We on this side probably have not as much occasion to quarrel with the hon. minister on that score as some of his colleagues. Those who were in this House in the last parliament will remember liow the House was startled when the Drummond County deal was taken in hand by the hon. minister. On that occasion there was question of the adoption of a line of policy involving a large expenditure, and coming naturally under the control of the Minister of Railways and Canals, but that unfortunate minister seemed to have been pushed to one side and in his place the Minister of Public Works conducted the negotiations and brought the deal to a successful issue. True the scheme met with rather a mishap when first presented, but on the second occasion, thanks to the vigilant care and attention of the Minister of Public Works, it went through. The hon. gentleman who, I am

glad to see to-day enjoying such good health, had occasion to absent himself one session, and his place was taken by the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock). I am sorry that some of the ministers from Ontario are not in their places to-night, because I should like them to hear what I have to say, even at the risk of offending them, regarding the invidious distinction that the Minister of Public Works enjoys to-day in the province of Ontario. In the riding I have the honour to represent, we tendered a banquet last year to that lion, gentleman, in which all joined irrespective of politics, and I think he was well pleased and so were we. But I have not heard of any banquets having been tendered any of the ministers from the province of Ontario. Were the Minister of Public Works to pass down any street in our town, he would be recognized at once by every one, but I cannot say the same of his colleagues from the province of Ontario, with the exception of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), whose doleful countenance, by reason of his picture having been before the public for the past twenty years, is rather familiar to our public. But were the other ministers from the province of Ontario to pass down the street of that town or any other towns on the shores of Georgian Bay, I doubt whether they would be recognized any more than any ordinary stranger. If there is a town in the whole country that has done honour to the Minister of Public Works in the shape of banquets, it is Owen Sound. Go to Collingwood, and you will find the same treatment accorded the Minister of Public Works there. Even if you go to that centre of Conservatives in Ontario, Toronto, you will find that the Minister of Public Works is really the only man in the public eye there to-day. The chief reason is that he is the power behind the throne, and both political men and the people recognize the faet that without his assistance we cannot hope to get anything in that great province. It is true that the ministers from Ontario have not much patronage at their disposal. There is first the Secretary of State (Senator Scott), who dispenses out the tape and the sealing wax, and whose countenance would be perfectly unknown, except by very few, were he to pass down King street, Toronto. He has no patronage at his disposal at all. Then we come to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who wanted to let the House know that he was still alive this afternoon, and broke for a few moments into verse. Perhaps he wants to spend the last of his days in this House because last session he and the late Minister of Justice were consigned to oblivion even by the back-bench members opposite. It was said last year that the Minister of Justice was soon to disappear from the scene, and now it is on the cards that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is about to be shelved into the lieutenant governorship of Ontario.

So that the great province of Ontario, which pays the bulk of the taxes of this country, is practically without representation in the cabinet, at least in the matter of patronage. Take the two great toll gatherers, the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock), and the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), whose daily duty it is to see where and how they can best exact taxes from the people- neither of these two has at his disposition any patronage at all. The Postmaster General is deserving of our special sympathy. Here is the Minister of Public Works taking the stand that it is within his power to give out contracts by days labour, as he does in Sorel to the tune of $125,000 per year, and yet the Postmaster General is helpless to give even a penny increase to a mail carrier. He has appeals from the letter carriers in all the great cities of the province, and he cannot move hand or foot. Yet the Minister of Public Works can deal out patronage by the hundred thousand dollars, aggregating in the year to millions of dollars, without any vestige of tender, and not a question is asked by hon. gentlemen opposite as to whether or not there is to be public competition for these loaves and fishes. Occasionally an hon. gentleman opposite will make a protest, and sometimes the kick results to their benefit. Why, I recollect that last session the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton), in a moment of audacity, dared to remonstrate with the Minister of Public Works with regard to one of his expenditures. What was the result ? With a good deal of finesse, the Minister of Pub'-lic Works managed to get him out of the way by having him appointed to a judgeship.
He was not treated very badly.

That is what I am pointing out. There are some gentlemen behind the Minister of Public Works to whom this example may be an incentive to go and do likewise. If they will only rebel against some of these expenditures they too may be slated for positions. I saw the other day that the junior member for Hants (Mr. Russell) is soon to be translated to a judgeship. It might be wise for him to make a spasmodic kick against the principle just laid down by the Minister of Public Works and obtain his reward all the sooner. Then, if the newspaper rumours are correct, the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Sutherland) is to be given a judgeship at an early day in order to smooth away some political troubles in his riding, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Justice promised the other day that there was to be a house-cleaning in the Ontario judiciary, and that a number of county court judges were to be retired, there is a vista open for the gentlemen of the legal profession on the other side of county court judgeships if not of Superior Court 22J
judgeships, and it would be well for them to take time by the forelock.
I congratulate the Minister of Public Works on the stand he has taken. In the first place, he has usurped the prerogative and rights of the Department of Railways and Canals. He went into the arena and tilted against his colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals, and dispossessed him. of what was most valuable in the Railway Department. And this summer the hon. gentleman made an incursion into the Department of Canals. The newspapers were filled with the accounts of the trips taken by the Minister of Public Works up French river with the view of bringing about the construction of a large public work there. The hon. gentleman really seems to bear a charmed life. He can do whatever he pleases. When the fight gets a little warm he simply smiles serenely, and the First Minister comes to his assistance. A few years ago, in Montreal, when a great political club, the Club Letellier, demanded that the head of the Minister of Public Works should be placed on a salver
It was not.

Certainly not. The minister sits there and smiles and knows that neither the premier nor any one else can put him out of his position. The papers have lately been discussing the separation of a pair of twins, which operation was performed in Paris, with the disastrous result that one of the twins died. The right hon. the First Minister will no doubt bear that in mind whenever there is any suggestion of his severing himself from the Minister of Public Works. In that event the consequences, I am afraid, would be even more serious, for, I believe instead of one they both would die.
But the Minister of Public Works was not content. Knowing the weakness of the Ontario ministers, he went to Ontario and ousted them from their own ground. When the party suffered such a defeat in the province of Ontario in the last election, when it came back with so many empty saddles, the Minister of Public Works decided that he himself would look after any future elections. He went up to North Bruce, but I did not hear of his being in West Durham at the last election. Perhaps it was because of the North Bruce defeat.
There is not a single matter that the Minister of Public Works brings before this House in open defiance of this cabinet that he does not put through. And he has proved that in the past. What happened in relation to what was known as the Kettle River Bill ? Here was the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in connection with an American company, which was pressing down to the border on the southern side of British Columbia. Day after day that

question was debated in tlie Railway Committee. It was a question of policy on tbe part of this government whether lines should be constructed from the American side into Canadian territory. A day was fixed when the Minister of Railways and Canals was to make a statement, and he stated at the time that the policy of the government was that the line should be constructed. That was directly adverse to the wishes of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Hon. gentlemen who were in the House at that time, will remember that memorable scene. The House voted, the yeas were called for on the Bill, one after another minister stood up on that side of the House and voted that the Kettle River Bill should be granted. But when it came to the Minister of Public Works he voted against it; and when the back benches were looked at, behold, to the humiliation of the premier, the Minister of Public Works had actually stolen from the premier himself his best and strongest supporters. Hon. gentlemen here remember that night when the Canadian Pacific Railway magnates were sitting in the gallery, and the Minister of Public Works kissed the tips of his fingers to them as much as to say, I am the whole government. There is not a doubt he was the whole government on that occasion.
Now there is great jealousy in the province of Ontario of the Minister of Public Works, and when by chance, owing to the illness of the Minister of Public Works and his absence in the old country, the Postmaster General was assigned to discharge his duties, what did the Postmaster General do on that occasion ? He caused to be sent out all over the province a famous circular asking what they required in their different ridings. Well, I think there can be no doubt that a great many answers were given to the Postmaster General. Whether the Postmaster General's information was acted upon afterwards I know not, but I do know that the Minister of Public Works was not at all pleased with the action of the Postmaster General on that occasion. For what did we see ? Why, we saw the Minister of Public Works threatening to do, what ? When the Postmaster General said it was the policy of any country, at least in modern times, to combine the postal and telegraph departments together, what did the Toronto 'Globe' say V Why, it said that that was right, and that the Postmaster General should have charge of the telegraph department. I would like to ask the minister of telegraph lines, I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works, if there is any prospect of the Postmaster General getting control of that department. Why, everybody knows that the Minister of Public Works has this matter right under his thumb, and that he has the whole control of this department. Yet, Sir, there is not a minister from the province of Ontario who will dare to stand up in his place and Mr. BENNETT.
condemn this principle, the principle that, while they were in opposition, they demanded should be carried out in its entirety. The Minister of Public Works snaps his fingers at them, and he expends, as he does at Sorel, $125,000 in day labour, and here is $15,000 at another point.
Now take the question of dredging, and that is rather a tender point with some gentlemen on the other side of the House; because, while none of them are owners of dredges-because if any gentleman on that side of the House owned a dredge he would be contravening the Independence of Parliament Act were he to engage in the work of dredging-the result is that some of them are owned by very near relatives of members of parliament. It may be avoiding the Act; but the general public don't think conduct of that kind is altogether free from reprehension. Now, what does the Minister of Public Works do on the question of dredging V This dredging work is not let out by public tender at so much a day, these dredges are hired for a time, and the work is given in that way. I am not going to say the work is not properly done, because I am not in the possession of information to justify me in making that statement. But I do say the whole principle is wrong, there should be public competition in all these matters, even when it is a question of this paltry $15,000. But it is the broader and greater principle that the minister has taken up this afternoon, that he for the future intends in his department- and I assume it is to spread in other departments-to act on his own will and pleasure, and is going to let out the public works he likes at public competition and open tender, but such as he does not like, he proposes to let out in the other way.
I quite agree with the statement of the Minister of Public Works, made, I think, in the city of Montreal, about the cabinet fighting like blazes. I think they should. I think when a Minister of Public Works infringes as he does on the departments of these other ministers, when he, in open day, red-handed, comes in and takes up the work of their departments, it is high time for these gentlemen to make a protest, as the Postmaster General made a protest, and as the Minister of Railways and Canals has made a protest too. In all this fighting, in all this tearing of hair, so to speak, that is going on, there comes up one feeble voice, and that is the voice of the Minister of Railways and Canals. Now, the Minister of Railways and Canals has caused to be published in the papers within the last day or two a statement that be is not going to retire from the cabinet. Well, it may be he is not going to retire of his own free will, but it must need be that the Minister of Railways and Canals believes that he is standing on slippery ground, or he would not pay so much attention as he does to the rumors that are

cent around the country to the effect that he is to be deprived of his position.
I am surprised that some gentleman on that side of the House don't enter a feeble protest. The other day, they had taken a minister away from the province of Prince Edward Island, there was a gentleman who name here who had held the rank of premier in Prince Edward Island. Yet despite the fact that the bulk of the representatives from that province are in accord with this government, in the most brutal way, this portfolio is taken away from that province. Then there is the great province of New Brunswick. The hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) came in here only last session with a great flourish of trumpets. He was to occupy a seat in the cabinet, but instead of his having the seat, the only gentleman who does occupy a seat in that cabinet is being assailed from behind, and he finds it necessary to rush into print in order to define his position while he is out of the House.
Now I hope that the Minister of Public Works, for the good of the country, will retract, or at least soften a little the statement he made this afternoon, I hope the Minister of Public Works will not alarm the public, because this statement will alarm the public. If the people of the whole Dominion are to be told that the Minister of Public Works is about to bring down large sums of money to be voted away, and that he is not going to ask parliament to harness these grants with the condition that open tenders shall be asked upon them, then I say it is going to be a matter of much comment and of great surprise to the people of the country. But how much greater will be the surprise when, from the great province of Ontario, with five ministers, there is not a single word of protest made by any one of them; and how much greater still the surprise that, with the array of talent from that province, there is not a single gentleman on the other side of the House who will stand up and protest against that principle. I have recalled the case of the late member of Kingston having made a remonstrance, and from the fact of his remonstrance having been beneficial, it may perhaps prompt some other gentleman on that side of the House to do the same. It is the principle that is being followed to which we object. I see my hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) who came into this House on a narrow majority, and if what I am informed is correct, his presence in this House was due greatly to the fact that a large public institution in the town of Cobourg just at the time of the general elections was being constructed by day's labour. This pernicious principle, this principle that hon. gentlemen have contended against in the past, is a principle that I hope, and still hope, some gentleman
opposite will rise and condemn in its entirety.

I understand the subject under discussion is as to whether public works should be done by public tender or whether, in certain cases, they should be done by day labour. It was said by an hon. gentleman this afternoon that in the city of Montreal there is very keen competition among contractors and that from that fact no doubt public work could be done with a large saving of expense by putting it up to public tender rather than by doing it by day labour. If that be true and if there is any saving by doing this work by public tender, you will often find that the saving in that way is at the expense of the labouring man and that is something that I do not think any hon. member of this House would wish to see. Now, independently of the question as to whether absolutely new works should be done by public tender or not, 1 submit that in the case of repairs to old buildings and the like of that it is far better to do it by day labour. Any one who has had experience in the matter knows how very difficult it is when you undertake to remodel or improve a building or to make additions to get plans and specifications with sufficient detail to provide for all the work that has to be done. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) who has just spoken, referred to the work which the provincial government has within the last two years been carrying on in Cobourg. It was known by many hon. members that some years ago the provincial government bought the old Victoria College building and that within the last two years they have been refitting that building for the purposes of an asylum. The way the work was done was this : the provincial architect made plans and specifications so far as he could of the changes that were necessary. An efficient man was put in charge of the work. The work was done by day labour, and while that work was going on I had an opportunity of visiting the place from time to time and what did I see ? I noticed that in many cases changes had been made even after the work had been commenced. A door would be changed to another location from the place it had been originally designed to occupy, showing clearly that it was impossible in a case like that to keep to the plans and specifications though they were prepared in the best manner possible. The architect would come down every two weeks, or every month, look over the work and suggest any changes that he considered necessary and proper. I have yet to hear any complaint, even among Conservatives, to say nothing of Liberals in that riding, as to the way in which that work has been carried on. The principle of tender was to a certain extent carried out. When materials were wanted, where it was practicable to put them up to tender, that was

done, and the materials in that way were purchased at the lowest price. I believe that on account of this work being done by day labour it has been far better done and at no greater expense than if it had been done by tender.
And you were elected.

It has been said by one hon. gentleman that I was elected by a narrow majority. But I see the hon.member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) in his seat, who lives in the adjoining riding, and he will know that my majority did not depend on Cobourg. True, I succeeded in getting a majority in Cobourg, but my total majority was 135, showing clearly that I was not elected on account of my majority in the town. Perhaps that will be considered a very narrow majority in a close riding such as this is, but we think it is a very good majority because my opponent had been elected in the riding, the same gentleman, since 1881 and during that time he had a number of by-elections and in every instance his majority was under one hundred, in the majority of cases ranging from 30 to 50.

If there was any argument needed to strengthen the conclusion that the system of doing work by day labour is wrong, the hon. gentleman (Mr. McColl), who has just taken his seat, has furnished it in his closing remarks that his riding has been represented since 1881 by his opponent and that this is the first time in the history of the constituency that it was carried by a Liberal, associated with the fact that at this particular time there was this work being done by day labour by the hon. gentleman's own friends and the admission that he makes himself that he frequently visited the work. Put these things together and he comes here as the result of it. Alluding to the admission that the system is a good one, it certainly is a good system for the purpose of manufacturing votes and sending the hon. gentleman down here. I think the hon. gentleman, when he reflects, will wish that he had not spoken, because, instead of doing his cause any good, he has done it very much injury. I was surprised at the announcement made by the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). I have always given him credit for being a very clearheaded man, and I have no very strong grounds to change that favourable opinion of him ; yet, when he announced that the system of constructing public works by tender was objectionable, and could not safely be carried out, I could not agree with him and I think the country will hardly agree with him. He said that if work were done, as it is done in England, or in France, it would be all right. Is he not here to adopt the English or the French system, if they are better than ours, of doing

work by public tender. Surely, if he discovered that there were objectionable features about our system he might have eradicated those features and improve the system of letting contracts by tender. If he found it serviceable and that it resulted in an economy of public funds he should have done it. But, he does not attempt to adopt this system. On the other hand, he has come to the conclusion that the letting of contracts by public tender is all wrong and that it is preferable to do work by the day labour system. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) places in my hand the Auditor General's Report and he gives me an opportunity of presenting to the House and the country an example of the benefits of the day labour system which the hon. Minister of Public Works has adopted. I have here the exependitures that were made down at the shops at Sorel. That is a place where the hon. minister spent last year over $125,000 by day labour. It was not as the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) recently said to patch up an old building at all. There may be some excuse if you are repairing an old building for not letting the work by tender, but this was not the patching up of an old building. It was building dredges and doing other work in connection with the shipyards at Sorel. Many of these works could easily have been let by tender because plans and specifications for them could have been got up beforehand and any one who understood the business might have been given an opportunity of tendering, with a reasonable hope of doing the work and knowing what he was doing. I find that there is no less than six hundred day labourers employed at Sorel. Imagine for a moment that there is a contest going on to elect a member, the same as there was in the riding of the hon. member for West Northumberland, "where there was a public work going on which was so useful to him, imagine 600 men in a riding employed under a government foreman, and what chance has the opposition candidate to be elected ? The Minister of Public Works has great ingenuity and great resources, and much stratagem while he is engaged in an election campaign, and no man better than he can use 600 voters under such circumstances to support the government candidate. Every one of these men are paid agents-I do not mean that they are paid in a wrongful way by being bought-but they earn their daily bread because of the employment afforded by the Minister of Public Works, and they are, to a certain extent, at his mercy, and we know that they have to vote as he wishes. Therefore, in such a constituency the opposition candidate has to start with a vote of 600 against him, not to speak of the relatives and friends of the workmen who may vote with them. The Minister of Public Works tells us to-day that the carrying on of public works by day's labour

is the better system, and that the contract system has been a failure, hut if he finished the sentence with the words which no doubt come to his tongue he would have added that the contract system was a failure-when he wanted to carry an election. Those men are employed on the work at a good round wage, and their work may not be very hard, but there are always a large number of applicants for any vacancy, and so the whole thing is engineered in order that every man who is working as well as every man who desires employment must be friendly to the government. The Minister of Public Works has spent $125,000 of the people's money in one year by the day's labour system, and let any ratepayer in the Dominion look over the pay sheets, and he will see the condition of things. The minister tells us that that money was economically and properly spent, but in my judgment the very reverse is the case. The announcement of the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that the tender and contract system has been a failure will be startling news for the country. When these gentlemen now on the treasury benches sat in opposition, the principle to which they most pinned their faith was that all public money, no matter how small, must be expended under the tender and contract system. They told us that was the only guarantee that the public expenditure would be safeguarded, and that those who were not friends of the government would have a chance of sharing in any public works. But the Minister of Public Works has changed his view on this point since he got into office. I believe that the people of the country will not endorse the Minister of Public Works in the views he has expressed to-day on this matter. I believe that the people of the country will say that the tender and contract system is the best means that has yet been devised to safeguard the expenditure of public money. I believe further, that a very large percentage of the ratepayers of Canada will differ from the minister on his day's labour theory. We have had unfortunate experience of the day's labour system all over the country. Look at that vote for building fences around the Levis quarantine station. I went all over that ground at L6vis and I saw these fences, and I believe that any practical farmer will tell you that these fences, for which a vote of $1,000 is asked, could be put in proper order for $200. Last year we spent $5,000 on this quarantine station, the year before we spent $5,000, and we are going on increasing our expenditure year after year. Under what system is that money expended ? It is expended on the day's labour system, that beautiful system that the minister has declared to the world to be the most economical and to give the best results. We are entitled to know how many rods of that fencing is to be done, of what material the fences is to be made, and what are the
specifications. The minister handed me over his book, but the chairman was so anxious to call out that the item was carried that I did not wish to cause delay. I am now sorry that I did not read out the information in that book to the House and thus do what the minister himself ought to have done. I remember very well that some years ago, when there was a vote for a post office in Renfrew or in the adjoining county, and when the Liberals were in opposition they took the whole night and a part of the day censuring the government for building a fence and a piece of a sidewalk. They wanted to know whether the fencing was hardwood or pine, what was the height, how much the lumber cost, and whether it was done by day's labour or by contract. They spent a whole night on that, and now it comes about that the Liberal government is spending five times as much in building sidewalks and fences around a piece of land twelve acres in extent, and they cannot or will not tell us what kind of fencing this is. As I said, I went over the ground at LSvis last year, and I believe if they asked between $50 and $100 for this work, instead of $1,000, they would have plenty of money to repair the fences. But I rose specially to call attention to the fact that the minister of the great spending Department of Public Works, has declared that the tender and contract system is a failure, and he gave us to understand by implication, although he did not say it in so many words, that he intends in the future to spend the public money by day's labour as much as possible. Well that is what he is doing at Sorel. If he carries out his intention he will have an army of his own friends engaged on public buildings in many of the constituencies throughout the country. If there is a by-election he will be sure to manipulate all that patronage for his own benefit. The government always manages that business very nicely. It was so in West Durham, it was so in Quebec, it was so in North Grey when they were trying to carry an election.
In West York.

I have no doubt from what I heard that the government were preparing for that kind of work in West York. The hon. member (Mr. Campbell) told the people that he was going to get them a post oflice and do numbers of other things if he only was elected. The reason he gave was that the Minister of Public Works and he were on friendly terms, and. that his opponent did not enjoy that distinction. It was something like what Mr. Hardy said at Owen Sound when he promised to get the people hot justice rather than cold justice. The election in West York was carried by such plausible promises as well as by other means, and it certainly was not carried by prayers, because the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) tells us that elections are not carried by prayers.

We want to know now, is the Minister of Public Works going to carry out the promises made by the member for West York (Mr. Campbell) during his election. The people of the country are getting a little sceptical of the promises made by the government and its supporters and they are anxious to see the goods delivered.
You did not stay very long in West York.

I did not notice my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) there at all. X was told that if he ventured to come there it might be too hot for him. I was in hopes of meeting my genial friend there, but I have no doubt he found it more convenient to stay outside the limits of the county. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that I am still in favour of letting contracts by public tender. I believe it to be the best system if it is properly carried out. The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has referred to a matter which is of considerable importance. In looking over the various portfolios held by the ministers, coming as I do from the province of Ontario, it is deplorable to find what little say the ministers from that province have in the management of the country, and in the expenditure of public money.
Look at the different departments. The fisheries were declared by the Privy Council to belong to the provinces; therefore the Department of Marine and Fisheries is comparatively speaking only an artificial department to-day with very little money to spend and very little patronage; and the hon. member for North Oxford (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has that department. Then, the Department of Trade and Commerce is held by the hon, member for South Oxford (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). That also is one of the; artificial departments, which the hon. minister himself a few years ago declared to be practically worthless, and to be retained only in order to provide a place for a friend of the government, though he manages to occupy the place very nicely and to draw the salary attached thereto; but there is no money spent and no patronage in that department. Then, there is the Department of Customs. It is true, the Minister of Customs has some patronage, but he spends very little money. The Postmaster General has a very valuable department, but he spends very little money, except in the way of giving contracts for carrying the mails. The Department of the Secretary of State is another artificial department. On the other hand, look at the great wealth of the province of Ontario, which is very properly called the first province in the confederation.
Next to Prince Edward Island.

Well, out of deference to my hon. friend, we will except Prince Ed-Mr. SPROULE.
ward Island. But the people of the province of Ontario furnish a great portion of the money that is spent by the government- that great province which is numerically so strong, and also so strong in its enterprise and ambition; and yet Ontario is not represented in this cabinet by a single minister who has control of the spending of any considerable amount of money. Where has it gone ? To the other provinces. Let the people of Ontario consider this. Why, the ministers from the great province of Ontario are relegated to about the lowest positions in the cabinet, where they have no money to spend, while the spending is left to the ministers from the other provinces, principally to my genial friend the Minister of Public Works, from the province of Quebec-and he loves to spend money. If there is one thing more than another that seems to be prominent ill his nature, it is his disposition to spend.
Except electioneering.

That is the next best thing he likes I will, by way of parenthesis, say one thing in his favour, that I believe lie makes a great deal of his expenditure where money ought to be spent- I give him credit for that.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. members to confine themselves as nearly as possible to the resolution before the committee.

For my part, I entirely dissent from the oft-repeated statement made this afternoon that the day labour principle is a wrong one or a bad one. It is easily conceivable that the administration of a principle may be wrong, and if the gentlemen wish to put it in that way, that would be a fair question for discussion; but to say that the principle is bad is not borne out by the facts. Evidence has been fast accumulating in the last few years endorsing the position that has been taken by the hon. Minister of Public Works when lie stated that he believes he could do work better and cheaper by the system of day labour, or the direct employment of labour, than he could by the contract system. Since the city of London about twelve years ago went wholly into this method of doing its work, most municipalities in the old country and the progressive municipalities in this country have taken hold of it, and it has been successful almost without any exception. Hon. gentlemen speak as if there were no drawbacks to the contract system-as if it were all perfectly satisfactory. I will venture the opinion that at least half the contracts which have been carried on under this government, whichever party is in power, have been unsatisfactory, resulting in more trouble and expense than you could imagine under any other system. The Minister of Public Works this afternoon, in speaking of the additions that have been made to this building, stated that they had been done by the day labour system, and that their cost had exceeded the estimates. He also said that circumstances had arisen which they could not see beforehand. If that work had been done by contract, what would have become of those matters which were unforeseen ? Would the contractor have attended to them for nothing ? He would either have been paid extra for them or the work would have been slighted. In the doing of work by contract, the contractor has to make money, and he has either to make it out of the labour, or out of the material, or out of the government. I do not by any means believe the statement that the people of this country are opposed to the direct employment system. Every trades council of this country- and there is one in nearly every city-is on record many times in favour of this system; the Dominion Trades Congress, which represents them all, is also on record in favour of it; and these are the men who do the work
-not the men who farm it out, but the men who actually do it, and these are the men who feel the pinch when the contractor has to make his profit. I want to tell the Minister of Public Works that if he puts this system into more active operation throughout this country, he will have the support of the people. The question of the direct employment of labour is very closely allied to that of public ownership, and I believe the public ownership idea is taking a strong hold of the minds of the people of this country. When some of these remarks were made this afternoon, I took from the mail an official communication from the city of Winnipeg, in which it is proved by figures that in the last few years that city has been performing one large public service which it took over, at 60 per cent less than it cost before, and another important service at 45 per cent less than it cost before; and all who have been in the city of Winnipeg know that these services are better carried out and the public are better served thanever was the case under the contract system. I firmly believe the people of the country are willing, even if the members of this House are not, to support the Minister of Public Works or any other minister who puts this prinicple into more general use.

I listened last session with a great deal of interest to what ! certain hon. gentlemen opposite had to say on the system of doing government works by day labour, and have followed their re-i marks this session with no less interest. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) gave two reasons why he objects to the principle of day labour. The first was that the men employed by the government got bigger wages and had a better time, and the second was that that method was cheaper and brought greater political benefit to the minister in charge. Well, I believe in the principle of day labour, and I desire to say that the Minister of Public Works, in carrying out this principle to the extent he does, is doing what the trade unions and labour organizations all over the country have been asking him to do for many years. What hon; members opposite have to prove, it seems to me, is not whether the government are deriving political benefit from the system, but whether or not the country is being deprived of any benefit and is suffering any injury by it. What does it matter to me if the government gain votes by conducting public works on the day labour principle ?
Oh, oh.

Hon gentlemen are laughing rather to early in the day. AVhat does it matter to the country if the government does gain votes, provided the work is well done and economically done. The Minister of Public Works has repeatedly told us that the work is better done, that It

is in every way more satisfactory, and we must accept his statement until his critics prove the contrary. As a matter of principle, X believe that so far as practicable the day labour method ought to be adopted, and let me tell the hon. minister that in adopting this method he is carrying out the views of organized labour in this country. When he sees that the labouring men are paid good wages, under the supervision of competent men, who will see that they give value for the money, he is doing what the people will support him in doing. I quite understand that it is not possible to carry out all the operations on government works by the day labour system, but there is a large percentage of that work which can be done on that system with great advantage to the country, and the greatest possible advantage to the people. So far as the views of organized labour are concerned, I can assure the Minister of Public Works that in the methods he has adopted he has the support of the people of this country.

During the discussion this afternoon, it was frequently stated that no evidence has been brought by the Minister of Public Works or by any one supporting his policy to show that the day labour system is cheaper and better than the contract system. Let me cite to the House some facts which will show that the position taken by the minister is in the interests of the country. I take my particulars from Yol. 2nd of the Auditor General's report, page V-212. Up to the present, the question has been one of sentiment rather than of fact, and the opinion which has prevailed in the country has been that the day labour system was not as cheap or as satisfactory ns the contract system. Well, every one judges by his own experience and personal knowledge, and I have some sympathy for hon. gentlemen opposite who speak from the knowledge they acquired when they were in office. It was they who built the Curran bridge, and they bulit it by day labour, and no wonder that system should appear to them very expensive when they look back to the history of that work. But I propose to cite two cases which will illustrate the difference between the cost of a public work done by day labour, when there was something to be made out of it for the boy, and one done by this government, when there was no question of anything of the kind. I refer to the building of two wharfs in the county of Glengarry-one at Summers-town by the late government and the other at Lancaster by the present government. The wharf at Summerstown was 85 feet long. The approach to the wharf was built of clay, shovelled up from either side, and simply dumping into the water 22 feet from the end of that dump, the cribwork was bridged over by timber on to the main pier, making actually not more than 63 feet and 22 feet of bridge work, or 85 feet alto-Mr. SMITH (Vancouver).
gether. The head of that pier was 22 feet wide and 120 feet long and the depth of water was 7 feet 6 inches.
At Lancaster, two years ago, there was another wharf built, 269 feet was the length. It was built entirely of stone. The stone was drawn from two to four miles, and there was not one load of earth in the entire approach. The depth of water was 8 feet 6 inches. The area of the landing head was about three times that of Summerstown wharf, the area of the approach was more than three times as long, and the cost of the wharf at Summerstown was $15,417, while that of the work at Lancaster was only $5,013. I submit to this House that here is a case that will stand comparison with any case which the opposition can bring forward. Here was the case of one wharf of less than one-third the size and built with a great deal cheaper material constructed by the old government, and it cost three times as much as this one constructed by day's labour under the direction of the present Minister of Public Works. There is no disputing these facts. It is not necessary that we should spend the whole afternoon talking about an abstract principle, when we have evidence to show what is being actually done. Because one administration did not, could not or would not, conduct public works cheaply that does not prove that this cannot be done by any administration. On the contrary, the fact is that these works are being done cheaply to-day, and the figures that I have given are proof of it. I venture to say that there is not a contractor who could see five cents of profit in that wharf at Lancaster, and the contractor wants to see a profit in every job he undertakes. If public works are conducted properly-and that is the kernel of the whole matter and I know that in my own county they are conducted properly- the principle at which we should aim is being carried out. If you have a foreman and an engineer to look after the work, this method of day's labour will give good results. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) complained that $125,000 was being spent for day's labour at Sorel. According to the figures I have given, the same work under the previous government would have cost $750,000.
Mi'. BROOK. You had better make It more than that.

No, I will not go a cent more. The hon. member for East Grey assumes that this work is done improperly. I have as much right to assume that the figures I have given are a fair comparison of the two administrations.
Will the hon. member (Mr. Schell) please explain how a work costing $125,000 under this government would have cost $750,000 under the old system ?
Because under the old system it would cost six times as much. 1 have given the figures-
Give us the facts.

I have given the facts also, and I defy any hon. gentleman to controvert anything I have said. If the former government had done things at Sorel on the same basis as they did them in the county of Glengarry, this work which now costs us $125,000 would have cost us $750,000. Merely because this amount spent at Sorel $125,000 is a large sum, these hon. gentlemen hold up their hands in horror. But they have not shown that any of this expenditure was extravagant or wrong.

We have listened to a very interesting discussion. The item under debate is $15,000 for the Montreal Examining Warehouse-addition to and alterations, including fitting, furniture, &c. The item seems very simple and clear, but the discussion has gone far beyond it. My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has gone all over creation. I do not intend to follow him. I hope the province of Ontario will not be alarmed by what he says. The poor, down trodden province of Ontario, represented by such feeble men as Sir Richard Cartwright, Mr. Mulock, Mr. Paterson and others-men of such inferior calibre-and with only five representatives in the cabinet. Hon. gentlemen who have spoken have said that Ontario was ahead in everything. If they will look at the figures, they will see that Ontario is ahead in expenditure also. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) complained that last year I spent $125,000 for day's labour. The hon. gentleman has made a mistake. I spent about four times that amount. I would ask the attention of the House to what we have done at Sorel, and what we are doing there. I did not invent the shipyard at Sorel-it was there when we took office. The government is spending upon the channel between Quebec and Montreal, about $75,000 to $90,000 a year. When the ship channel was handed over to the government in 1888, there was handed over also an inferior fleet of dredges, stone lifters and other craft. With this outfit, the work on the channel was conducted at a great disadvantage. The trade of the country was expanding and the people insisted that we should develop the country's waterway. What was I to do ? Was I to import dredges ? Hon. gentlemen oposite are daily reproaching the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) because, having no equipment to build cars and locomotives, he has been obliged to import cars and locomotives from the United States. Was I to do the same 7 Not by any means. I did not take that course, nor do I intend to do so. Whether I am here for a long time or a short time,
while I am here, every piece of work for my department that can be done in this country shall be done here. That is the policy I carried out in Sorel. We have built a magnificent fleet of dredges there. Ought I to have imported dredges as my predecessors did. There are three dredges-in the maritime provinces, the ' St. Lawrence,' the ' Canada ' and the ' George Mackenzie,' which were imported from England. These dredges cost in round numbers $120,000 each, and their capacity is not more than 1,000 yards a day. We have built at Sorel dredges with a capacity of 7,000 or 8,000 yards a day each and with less cost, built them by Canadian labour and of Canadian material as far as possible. If I am wrong, I am prepared to stand by the wrong I have done. The great work of deepening, widening and otherwise improving the channel between Montreal, Quebec and the gulf could not possibly be carried on without a shipyard. Anybody who has had experience in work of that kind knows that if you have dredges, stone lifters and tugs, accidents and breakages occur every day, and you must have a shipyard, just as every well equipped railway company must have a workshop for the repair of its locomotives and cars.
I have done that, and my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) would have done the same thing. And where is the wrong of doing these works on Canadian soil, with Canadian hands ? What wrong, I ask again, have I committed ? I have done right, and my hon. friends opposite are mistaken in their criticism. We are carrying out a great public work. My hon. friend says we are employing in Sorel 600 hands. We are not employing quite as many ; on an average we employ about 400 hands, sometimes less but never more, in building dredges, tugs, and in works of all kinds. Now these are Canadians, and as I say, the work is done on Canadian soil. Now if there is any other way in which that work could be done I would like to know it. I would like to know how the St. Lawrence can be deepened and widened except by having a shipyard in which to make the repairs that are necessary.	.
If my hon. friends will allow me to say so, they are altogether mistaken in saying that it is in the interest of a government to carry out works by contract. A minister who was not entirely honourable would make a lot of money out of contracts, and by giving extras. That could be done. He cannot make a dollar in giving out a work by day labour. He has no chance to do anything. The labour is paid every day, and the minister has nothing to do with it. Why, I ask again, should the labouring men of this country be deprived of their honest earnings in order that the contractor might earn millions ? Politically there is nothing to be gained from day labour. But, on the other hand, the contract system gives a lot of

trouble. When a contract is given a minister always has a great deal of trouble. I say again, backed up by an experience of five years and a half, that on many occasions public works are better carried out by day labour than by contract. I do not lay down the rule that the system of tenders must be put aside. I never said that, I do not say it now. But I say that if X were able to find everywhere competent foremen I would not hesitate to carry out the largest work by day labour.
My hon. friends have forgotten past history. Doubtless the new members of this House are surprised to hear this debate. But this is not the first time a similar debate has taken place, we hear it every year. My hon. friends opposite forget their own past when they scarify me because I am asking $15,000 for some repairs in Montreal. The ex-Minister of Finance in the Conservative government carried out, in the city of St. John, works of repair and rebuilding a custom-house to the tune of $200, 000, by day labour, and he did not lose the confidence of my hon. friends opposite. I gave to the House a day or two ago a complete list of all the works that had been carried out by day labour. I do not mean by any means to shield myself behind the example of my predecessor. I say again that on many occasions a public work can be better done by day labour than by tender and contract. My hon. friend asked me why I did not change the system since I did not find it good. I am not strong enough to do so ; and my hon. friends opposite would not sustain me if I attempted to make the change, and if I attempted to make the system of tender perfectly safe.
I will if the hon. gentleman will convince me.

There are days when my hon. friend is pretty hard to convince. Suppose I were to prepare a list of the contractors whom I would invite to tender for public works. What would be the result in this House ? I never could get five cents of estimates through. I would be told that I had picked odt a list of partisans. No, Sir, I am not strong enough to do that. In England, France and Germany the system has been established, and it works well. Now, Sir, compare the two systems of day labour and of contract. Where are the scandals in connection with day labour that we have seen in connection with contracts ? There may be some mistakes, I do not say there are not. But if you look at what has been done in connection with large contracts you will find some pretty hard things.
I do not think that the time taken in this discussion has been wasted. My hon. friend said that I was extravagant in the expenditure of money. Permit me to say that he is wrong. I am not afraid of a wise ex-Hon. Mr. TARTE. *
penditure of money. I am rather sanguine of the future of this country, and when I am convinced that an expenditure of money will promote the progress and prosperity of Canada, I do not hesitate a moment. One thing that this discussion will promote is progressive ideas. This century is a century of progress. When I happen to be Minister of Public Works, and have around me men of great ability, I do not like to be told that any contractor in Ottawa or Toronto is more able than I am to direct a great public undertaking. I do not like it. I do not like to be told that the Canadian artisan is not quite as able to do work by day labour under my direction as he would be under the direction of a foreign contractor. So I say time has not been wasted in this debate. The country will listen to this debate. That large and important class of workingmen will not lose sight of what has been said to-night on both sides of the House.

This question has been discussed nearly all the afternoon, and I do not think I can throw much light upon it. But I am certain of one thing, and that is that all the' work this government requires to be done cannot possibly be let by contract. There must be some work done by days' work. The messengers in this House, the pages, and all classes of employees around this building, must be hired by the day. So it is with a great deal of work which the Minister of Public Works requires to be done. I think a similar discussion took place last year, and I said then that I believed that work could be done cheaper and better by day labour in many cases than by contract. There is one trouble in day labour, and I think that is what hon. gentlemen on this side of the House complain of most. I understand that when the present members of the government sat on This side of the House they complained bitterly against the very thing that they are doing now.
Now, if that be true, they are not consistent, but the question is : Are they right ? I think under the circumstances they are right, and I think that it would have been better for this country to have work done by the day, but they must see that they have good foremen, not political hacks, not men that are working for themselves and their job, but men that would see that the country is well served and when a man does not discharge his duty, no matter how good a politician he may be, he should be discharged. One trouble arises as the result of the government doing all this work by day's labour because the government have a strong pull on every man that they hire by the day, just the same as the manufacturers control their workmen, as we all know. There is another point to be remembered. We all know that the contractors are the most liberal subscribers to party funds, and the gov-

eminent will be deprived of this assistance if the work is done by day's work. Now, I think this discussion has gone far enough.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words in reference to the illustration which was given us by the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) and referred to by the hon. Minister of Public Works as an example of what might be done by day's labour. That was the Curran bridge, which was cited as a justification for doing work by day's labour. Why, that whole job was done by day's labour and the contention of hon. gentlemen who sat on this side of the House at the time the inquiry took place was, that the cost of the work was three or four times as much as it would have been had it been let by contract. The whole argument against the government was that they did not let it by contract.
The labour was given out by contract.
On the Curran bridge 1
Yes.
Not at all.

Yes, St. Louis had the contract for the whole of the labour.
Mi1. SPROULE. He was given a schedule of prices that would be acceptable to hire men at, and he made as much out of it as he liked, but the whole contention in that case and the whole force of the argument against the government was based on the fact that they had not done the work by public tender. Now, this is cited to-night as an example of what might be accomplished by day's labour. The hon. gentleman who just took his seat says that we cannot do all public work by contract. There is no person who ever contended that we could. The argument of hon. gentlemen now supporting the government, when on this side of the House was, that when the government departed from the principle of doing work by public contract they departed from a salutary and correct principle, and that just in so far as the government departed from that principle they did wrong. To-day, they are converts to another theory, the same as they are in many other lines, since they occupied the treasury benches. The hon. Minister of Public AVorks shakes his head. I never heard him advocating the adoption of the day-labour system before he became a minister of the Grown. But now, the hon. minister says that he has built dredges at Sorel and he asks if he had not a right to do it. So far as he could employ Canadian labour, put in Canadian materials and do the work at the proper price, I have no objection in the world, but I ask him, if that be correct, why he gave a contract to Mr. Bertram, of Toronto, for the
building of a dredge, and will he tell us what that work cost ?
The shipyard in Sorel was not well enough equipped then for the building of a big dredge like that, because our hands were full. AVe had too much work on hand.
AVill the hon. gentleman tell us that he could have done that work cheaper than he had it done by tender ?
I could not say that I could have done it cheaper, but certainly as cheap.
The other feature of the argument which he presented was that he was employing Canadian labour. AVhat did Mr. Bertram employ-American labour ?
No, Canadian labour.

AA'hat material did he put in ? Did he not employ Canadian labour and put in Canadian material just the same as the hon. minister did at Sorel ?
