Therefore, that argument amounts to nothing, because, although the contract was let by tender to a man in Toronto, he employed Canadian labour and put in Canadian material. I think if we were to endeavour to convince the country that the contract cost more than it should have cost, the hon. Minister of Public AVorks would be the first to defend his action and to say that it was the cheapest contract ever carried out in Canada. I am quite sure it was. He says that he never brings in American dredges. I do not like to bring to his attention an instance of where he did, but I think he brought one into Collingwood.
No, I did not say that I never brought in American dredges at all.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he did so. However, I am not going to make an argument out of that, because I think he did right there. It was needed, he had none of his own, he got a dredge where he could and he employed it. If there ever was an attempt made to educate the people of this country up to the belief that the proper principle of doing work was by tender and contract, it was made by the hon. Minister of Public AVorks and his friends, who are going back on that principle to-day. I only want to draw attention to the inconsistency of these hon. gentlemen in this particular, as in many others. I have a few words to say to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith). He presented to us the most astounding principle. What does it matter, he says, if the electors are bought up when you employ them by day's labour. What does it matter if the members of this House are all elected by corruption ?

I -would like the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) to complete the sentence.

I took down the hon. gentleman's words. He said : What does it matter to the country if the government make votes by spending money in this way ? What are they doing if they are makipg votes but corruptly buying them ? What does it matter if this House is purchased and put here ? What does it matter to the people of the country ? We have too many [DOT]evidences of corruption during the last few years. We are getting rapidly from bad to worse, and it is a question which may be very properly asked how much of the present system of spending public money is chargeable for the corruption we have in the country to-day ? When the hon. member for Nanaimo advances that most astounding doctrine that it does not matter, I can tell him that the great moral sentiment of the country will not agree with him, that -the great moral sentiment of the country is against that principle, because this country desires to be represented in an honest parliament, not a purchased one, not a venal one, not one bought with public money by day's labour. It does matter, it is a matter of very great importance not only to this House, but to the country, and we all hope the day is far distant when any other man will be found who will stand up in the House and defend a measure for buying up the electorate by spending public money in this way.

Before this discussion closes I would like to say a few words as I have had considerable to do in carrying out the principle of day labour. It was my experience in a western city, the city of Winnipeg, for five or six years, being in the city council, to know how this system has worked out. Most of our work during the years from 1880 to 1895 had been done by contract. It was found that most of the sewers were defective in construction and material; it was found that large sums were claimed for extras, and expensive law suits resulted from this contract system. The people asked themselves ; Is there a better system to be adopted, and consequently the day's labour system was started at first on a small scale. It was found that it worked well. It was then inserted in all contracts given by the city that the minimum wage paid should be 174 cents per hour. Some of the contractors tried to evade that clause, but finally they were compelled to carry it out, and so the work went on. Many of our wealthy merchants who at first objected to the' day's labour system are now the strongest advocates of that system, and the consequence is that wherever work is done now in the city of Winnipeg it is done by day's labour. We were told that the asphalting of the streets could not be done by day's labour, Mr. SPROULE.
but we said :	Surely if the contractors
can bring experts from St. Louis or Detroit, we can hire them just as well. To-day we have our own asphalt plant, we have our own experts, and all that work is done by cur own men. We were told that we could not get the stone in proper shape, but we bought our own quarry, we built our own railway to the quarry, we got our own engines and cars, and at the present time we are laying streets in the city of Winnipeg as cheaply as anywhere in the United States or in England, (considering the cost of living), and in addition to that we are laying better streets. Then again, another good result followed. It was found that after the day's labour system was adopted we had no more defective sewers. There is no complaint to-day that sewers are caving in. I say, all honour to the Minister of Public Works if in this progressive age he is trying to carry out the principle adopted in the many progressive cities of the United States and of Great Britain- the principle of doing public works by day labour rather than by contract labour. There is another feature of this question that has not been alluded to. I refer to the charge made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I do not think he represents the Conservative party in that charge, because if he does it is one of the most disgraceful reflections on the workingmen of Canada that has ever been uttered in parliament. He said that the moment you employ a man and pay him $1.75 a day you buy him up politically body and soul for ever. Well, we have 1,500 men almost constantly on the pay roll of the city of Winnipeg, and we expend nearly $1,000,000 a year, and there is not a citizen of Winnipeg who will say that those men are bought in municipal or national politics, because they get a minimum wage of 174 cents an hour. If you can corrupt workingmen by paying them $1.75 or $2 per day, how much more could you corrupt the contractor who would be at the head of these men if he got that contract. If it is buying up and corrupting men to pay them a fair living wage under the day labour system, then it would be buying them up and corrupting them wholesale under the contract system. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) cast a reflection on the workingmen of Canada that they will resent at the proper time, when he made the statement that [DOT] workingmen employed by day's labour were bought up body and soul.
The hon. member for East Grey did not make that statement. The member for East Grey did not say anything of the kind.

Here are your words. You said that when the opposition candidate goes to a riding where 600 men are employed on government works by day's labour

he starts out with a majority of 600 votes against him.
Yes, and I repeat it.

The discussion arose this afternoon on an item of $15,000 for adding a new story to the examining warehouse in the city of Montreal. It is on behalf of the builders and contractors of that city and of the labourers themselves that I appealed to the Minister of Public Works to adopt what is the right course, and to let this work out by contract after calling for tenders in a proper manner. That would give to every man in the city of Montreal who is a builder, and to every workingman of the city of Montreal a chance of taking part in that work. I have heard nothing in the discussion to change my mind on this subject. Since this government has been in power-I do not know, nor am I responsible for what occurred before- it is a well known fact in the city of Montreal where there is such keen competition among the builders and where there are such able workmen; it is a well known fact that only a certain clique of builders can get any work from the government. That is what we object to. It is a well known fact that these contractors, or those who have charge of work for the government are often obliged to employ men who are not first-class workmen. That is the abuse X i>rotest against. There is not a corporation, there is not a business man in Montreal, or in Toronto, or in any of the large centres, who, if he had a story to add to a large building, would not call for tenders publicly and give the work to a contractor. I venture to say that the large amount of money spent by this government for advertisements, when it chooses to advertise for public tenders, might very properly be kept for other purposes, because I believe that if government works were properly advertised in the ' Canadian Official Gazette' every necessary opportunity would be given to contractors to tender, and these works would be executed for half what they cost under the present system. That stands to reason. Who is best qualified to erect an additional story to the examining warehouse in Montreal ? Is it not the man who Is accustomed to that work, who under proper conditions would be obliged to put his prices as low as possible in competition with other builders, and who would be obliged to do work of the first quality; or, is it the official sent down by the government who will start out on this work employing men who are half the time political friends of the government and half the time unfit for the work which they are set to perform-? It stands to reason that when the work is given by tender under proper conditions, it will be better done, more expeditiously -done and more cheaply done. X have heard a great deal from the Minister of Public Works in reference to the works he has
executed at Sorel. I do not know that any member on this side criticised the establishment of the works at Sorel. It is very proper for this government which has so culpably neglected the navigation of the St Lawrence notwithstanding the continuous demands made by the shipping interests and underwriters of Montreal; it is very proper that one of the members of this government who has had some energy should claim some merit for having established the works at Sorel. Nobody objects to that. Nor does any one object to the payment of the employees there fair wages no more than we would object to the payment of fair wages to those who are employed in Ottawa. But the principle which we condemn is that principle which leads the Minister of Public Works to purchase all the wood required in this ship-building yard without calling for tenders, and by reason for which we have to pay exorbitant prices for the supplies. It is undeniable that the minister could get wood of better quality probably, and certainly at a lower price if he advertised for tenders for the supplies required at Sorel. What we find fault with, and what we condemn also is, the purchasing of the hardware supplies without public tender. We condemn the system of placing these orders at exorbitant prices with favourites of the government and with men who are not even hardware merchants but who purchase the hardware required on commission. That is what we object to. In England and the United States when such supplies are required a list is sent to all those engaged in the trade, and each article has a fixed price opposite which the government will pay. Is not that a progressive system V Is it not a better system than which the Minister of Public Works has adopted of giving orders to political friends, without giving others engaged in the trade a chance to tender. We have many excellent hardware establishments in Montreal and why is not the same favour extended to alT? As to dishonesty, I believe there is no question but that every opportunity is given to a dishonest minister or to a dishonest government to derive indirect profit from the expenditure of public funds under this system. The workingmen of Montreal are interested in seeing that public money is expended wisely and economically because they are contributors to the public treasury just as much as we are. The workingmen have to protect them the clause which insures that they shall be paid a fair wages, and does the hon. member from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) believe for a single instant, that when work is given out in the slovenly way in which it is given now, the workingmen will be surer to receive fair wages than if it was given out by contract to the lowest tenderer under a contract which includes the fair-wage clause. The hon. gentleman from Vancouver (Mr. Smith? and the

hon. gentleman from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary have stated that all these public works should be done by day's labour, but if they think that now, why did they not take the same position at the recent meeting of the Trades and Labour Congress. My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Smith) made a report to that congress and among the many things which he considered necessary for the welfare of the workingmen he made no reference to the disappearance of the contract system. I find his name as president of that congress signed at the foot of a report, which purports to mention the grievances complained of by the workingmen of Canada. There is not one single word in that report in support of the theory which the hon. gentleman is contending for to-day, that public works should be done not by contract, but by day labour. On the contrary, if the members of this committee will take the trouble to read that report, they will find that in it my hon. friend practically approves of the contract system, provided the fair-wage clause is inserted in the contract and observed.
Will the hon. member read the statement ?

There is at page 17, clause 8, a statement under the heading, ' current or fair wages on government contracts.' I will with pleasure read the whole clause, but I do not think I would be justified in taking up the time of the committee in doing so. The gist of the report upon that particular point is that the government system of giving out public works by contract has been satisfactory where the fair wage clause has been not only inserted but observed ; and the report goes on to say that in cases where that clause has not been observed, the matter has been brought to the attention of the government, and the claims of the labouring men have been recognized and paid by the government. The labourers under the day labour system will not be paid higher wages than the fair wage clause provides for, and if the work is done by contract and the fair wage clause is observed, the workmen lose nothing. But my hon. friend had other grievances against the government. He signed a report which stated that the alien labour law, which this side of the House strove last year to have amended, had not been properly observed. There is also a complaint against Chinese immigration in British Columbia. But there is not a single word on the question which my hon. friend this evening seemed to regard as essential. I believe, as the hon. Minister of Public Works says, that this discussion has not been useless ; and if it is a consecrated principle of this government that public works ought not to be done by public tender and contract
No one has said that.

The Minister of Public Works stated this afternoon that he believed as a general rule that works were better executed by day work than by public contract. I believe there are some works which cannot be executed by contract; but the item to which I called attention this afternoon is just one of those cases in which, if he has prepared his specifications and the officers of hist department estimate it at $15,000, I will find in the city of Montreal contractors who will do the work for a much lower figure.

What is the use of making so much noise over such a little affair ! My hon. friend has tried to prove that I should do by contract certain works in Montreal. What is the size of these works ? Building alterations and additions costing $8,000. On hearing him, the House would have concluded that it would have been more like a work costing a quarter of a million.
It is the principle.

Now, the chief architect of the Department of Public Works is one of the most practical men that any minister could have at his disposal. Mr. Ewart started life as a mason; he has worked in the ordinary way that workingmen do ; he has learned his trade, and he has climbed the hill by his labour, his ability and his honesty. Now, he has prepared all the specifications of these works, and that small work cannot be carried out for less than $6,000. It is composed largely of alterations inside the building- taking down walls and improving the lighting of the examining warehouse which is now too dark. That work cannot be done by' contract, because no man who has any knowledge of building and repairing work could say exactly what it should cost. Then, there is $4,000 for furniture and fittings. These cannot be bought by contract. Surely the Department of Public Works can buy furniture and fittings to that extent. My hon. friend says that he does not object to the Department of Public Works having workshops at Sorel; but he insists that all purchases should be made in an honest way. I share his view ; but I say that there are a sufficient number of traders and merchants in any party to afford competition. But I would say more than that. On many occasions at Sorel we have bought goods from firms who are not friends of this government. Of course, when my officers are able, all things being equal, to buy from friends of the government, they do so. That is not only their right but their duty. But when we cannot buy all things with equal advantage from friends, we go elsewhere. For instance, Fotheringham & Workman are not the friends of the government, but they are a reliable firm, and we have purchased goods from them. But I say that

*where I am able to buy from political friends 1 do so, after having asked for tenders-not public tenders, but tenders such as all first-class firms ask for. Now, I am surprised that my hon friend, who lives in Montreal, does not remember what takes place there. I am not the only man who carries out large works by day's labour. The shipyards of Sorel are after all nothing compared with the large works which the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway have in Montreal, and. which they are carrying on by day's labour.
Does the hon. minister think that they purchase wood or any other material without calling for tenders ?

I will come to that point. But my hon. friend cannot deny that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are building locomotives and cars in Montreal by day's labour. The Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway do not advertise publicly for their goods. I challenge my hon. friend to produce one instance in which the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway advertise for their supplies. They have a purchasing agent just as I have, who goes from firm to firm and asks for prices. I am doing what all the large firms do and what any sound business man would do.

Judging by some of the speeches made on the opposite side, we are charged with being opposed to a system of day labour. I want to remind the Minister of Public Works that some years ago the very position he now takes was taken by the Conservative government, and on that occasion he opposed the policy which he now advocates. I remember distinctly then making the statement, which I repeat now as a member of this opposition, that I was not opposed to day labour on certain works, because, in my judgment, you cannot on such works call for tenders and let them by contract. But on all new works, I take the ground to-night as I did then, that it is in the interests of the people to call for tenders and give the work out by contract. And in that contract there should be a stipulation compelling the contractor to pay the rates of wages ruling in the districts where the work is done. That was the stand I took then and which I take now.
Some hon. gentlemen have argued that the contract system is a very bad one, and that the day labour system has everything in its favour. But the minister himself says that the contract system has some advantage to the ministers and that the day labour system has none. From that statement I presume there must be some profit derived from the contractor who gets the contract, and I have yet to meet the contractor in this country who is willing to put his hand into his pocket and pay out his money for nothing. Unless there should be a minister whom he can approach in that way, in order 23
to secure a very profitable contract, there would be no profit to the minister in giving a contract to any contractor who did not pay something in order to secure it.
With regard to the day labour system, let me cite an instance to show how it sometimes worked. Some years ago a fire occurred in the western block and there was an election in Pontiac county. Well, on the building injured by the fire there were workingmen as thick as flies in summer on a sugar mound, and the main object in putting them on that work was to secure their votes at that election. And I remember making in this House the statement with respect to that very block, that a certain supporter of the government had been passing with me and observed the workmen lifting a stone and taking nearly an hour to lift it, and that he remarked that he did not at all approve of that style of doing work. The Minister of Public Works challenged my statement. I said if he wanted one of his followers behind him to be a witness against him I was quite willing to state who the gentleman was. But the Minister of Public Works did not insist. It was a very strong supporter of the government who had found fault on that occasion with the way the work was being done.
Let me give another instance. Every hon. gentleman in this House has seen that little summer house in the square outside. Well, no less than eight painters were employed on that little building, and no less than $600 spent repairing it, which practical men in the House said ought not to cost $100.
With respect to the platform of the Trade and Labour Council, I am one of those who are not particular about the good opinion of that council. Let me tell you why. There are men in that Trade and Labour Congress in whom I have not much confidence as there are others in whom I have considerable faith. I am somewhat of the opinion of a delegate, who was sent as a representative from Toronto last year, and who in Toronto declared on his election card as his chief plank that he was opposed to government ownership of that congress. The manner in which that congress is usually conducted is not unknown to the public. It is well known that the congress is manipulated by government employees, who are there to protect the interests of the government in order to get the support of the workingmen of Canada. And these gentlemen entertain so high a regard for me that when an election is on in my constituency, they take the stump against me. Yet notwithstanding their efforts I have managed to retain so far the confidence of those I represent.
I do not think that my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) and my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Smith), who profess to be the leaders among the labouring men, entirely express the views of the workingmen when they say they are completely in



favour of the day labour system on all public contracts. Notwithstanding the plank in the platform of the Trades and Labour Congress, I maintain that there is a large number of workingmen who contribute their share of the taxes, and in whose interest it is that the public expenditure of the country shall be as little as possible. They are men who never expect to get employment on public works, and it is as much in their interest that these contracts should be let to the lowest tenderer, subject to a fair provision regarding wages, as it is in the interests of any other class of the community.
But how does that day labour system work ? In my constituency there is a public work being erected, but on that work not one Conservative workingman can find employment. I refer to the work at Port Stanley. That is not what the workingmen of this country want to be done. They do not want any distinction drawn between men of different politics. They do not want to see the employment exclusively given to Liberals and refused to Conservatives. For that reason, if for no other, I would oppose the day labour system entirely. I am in favour of doing by day labour work which cannot be given out to contract, but in the ease of all new work I believe in the contract system.
My hon. friend speaks of the public works at Sorel, but there is a great distinction between those works and a public building, say in the county of Bothwell. Suppose there was a post office being erected at Wallaceburg, will any man pretend that you can put that on the same basis as the works at Sorel ? In the one case I should approve of doing the work by contract, in the other case, I should approve of doing it by day's labour. That is my position.

I do not want to take up the time of the House-I am not in the habit of doing so. But after what has been said, I think it is necessary for me to make some little explanation. This is not the first time that the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has attempted to depreciate officials of the Trades and Labour Congress who are not in a position to reply to him.
I have made no attack on them.

Last session, when similar matters to this were under discussion, the hon. member made special reference to men who were employed by this government as being representatives to that congress, and there is not an Ontario man in this House who did not know whom the hon. gentleman meant. Why should not an employee of this government be a representative to the Trades Congress ? Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) support the idea that, because a man labours for the government he ought not to belong to a labour association ?
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith, Vancouver) wish me to answer ? I can tell him that if he would not support the government's interest he would not be the government's representative.

I have said before, and I say again, that it is something to say for this government and for the independent men who work for it that those men are at perfect liberty to be members of that congress and to take part in the discussions which are intended to result in good to the workingmen of this country. Now, I desire to say a word, in explanation, to the hon. gentleman for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). That hon. gentleman preached me a little sermon about the moral standards of this government. I would support that hon. gentleman or any other man in keeping up those standards. But I confess that I do not think much of the moral standards of an hon. member who will criticise the statement of a fellow member and will give the House the impression that he sets forth that statement when, as a matter of fact, he reads only one-half the sentence in which it is set forth. When the hon. gentleman read half the sentence and passed judgment on the proposition, he did as unfair a thing as any hon. gentleman could do.
I took down the sentence at the time and read every word of it.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I had to rise and request him to read the sentence, and it was not until I did so that he read it. I will read the sentence myself, as I want it to be put down. What I said was this : ' What does it matter if the government do get votes, if they get them as a consequence of money well spent and of good service to the country ? ' Why, does not the hon. gentleman know that this is the principle that makes all votes ? The people of this country are voting all the time for a government that will give them good service and do good work. That was exactly what I meant. I repeat that the hon. Minister of Public Works has proven that the day's wages system renders to the people of this country good service, and, as a result, the people are sure to support the government. What objection would any one have to that ? I hope the hon. minister will maintain his principle, that he will take advantage of every opportunity to use it where it can be used with economy and with good service to the country. And I repeat again that the organized labourers of this country will support the government that supports that principle.
Public Works-chargeable to income-public buildings-Quebec-Montr ;al public buildings- improvements, alterations, repairs, &c., $8,000.
What repairs are these '!
The general repairs to these other buildings, not the examining warehouse.

I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the state of affairs in Montreal as regards public buildings. The hon. minister will remember that during the last parliament I showed the large amount that we spent every year for repairs to the public buildings in Montreal, and also the large amount in rentals for offices of Dominion government officials. This is not only expensive, but it means that the officials are separated, instead of all being in the same building. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) when he comes to Montreal, and the other members of the government when in Montreal, are obliged to use a room in the post office building. I believe that all this could be cured and money saved if the government would listen to the complaint that is made in Montreal as to the insufficient size of the post office. I really think that, as Montreal contributes such a large amount to public revenue, the government should seriously consider whether it would not be rendering justice to the people by listening to these complaints. If the government would build a new post office or enlarge the present one, I believe it could provide better accommodation for its officials, and at the same time save money and give satisfaction all round.

I am obliged to confess that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) is about right. The Montreal post office is too small. My hon. friend and colleague the Postmaster General has under consideration a system of sub-post offices which he hopes to bring into effect in Toronto and Montreal. In Toronto, the post office is even worse than that of Montreal. That is not my fault-I have not been in office very long. One trouble about carrying out the project of the Postmaster General is that land in Montreal is so dear. I tried a few days ago to get an option on certain property. I acted with all the secrecy possible, and I find that the prices asked are very high. I think the system the hon. gentleman suggests would not be a success.
Quebec Immigrant building on Louise Embankment and Breakwater, and King's Wharf Building, $2,000.

The foundations of the building are giving away, and we have to renew them.
Quebec Military buildings-new iron foundry, inclusive of electric light plant and sundry machinery ordered, $7,000.
In this matter I suppose I am doing right, because we are asking for tenders for this work and the one last mentioned.

How do you need a foundry there ?
23i

It is for the cartridge factory. In this case I am building on plans approved and prepared by the Department of Militia and Defence. Military matters are calling for a good deal of attention of late years, and the Department of Militia and Defence require these works to be done. The money was voted last year, but we did not spend any.
Is this the only establishment for the manufacture of military material in Canada ?

I think so.
St. Hyacinthe drill hall $5,000.
Has a site been chosen for this drill hall ?
No, nothing has been done so far.
A part of this sum was voted last year, has nothing been spent ?
No, we expect to spend up to the 1st of July $5,000. _

My hon. friend is aware that the question of this site is causing a good deal of discussion in St. Hyacinthe. I am not acquainted with the details, but my hon. friend probably is. Is the city going to contribute a site for the drill hall ?
No.
Does my hon. friend know where it is proposed to build ?	.
We have not yet made up our minds.

I think before voting such a large amount-and we will probably have to vote considerably more before the drill hall is finished-we are entitled to know where it is going to be. My hon. friend must be aware that there is a considerable difference of opinion in St. Hyacinthe as to where the drill hall should be located. If he is not able to give us some information to-night, and as he expects to find out in a day or two, I would ask him to let the item stand.

I would ask the hon. gentleman not to insist upon that, because such an objection is never taken. We will take the money, and parliament has enough confidence in us, generally speaking, to let us choose the site after getting the money. I cannot accept that principle at all, because sometimes it takes considerable time to make choice of a site. I will consult with the military authorities, and I may have to go there myself. On several occasions I have gone and examined sites before making a choice.

I am not prepared to accede to the principle that we should be asked to vote an amount for a drill hall in a case where the site is in dispute, without knowing where that drill hall is going to be placed.
How can you select a site without getting the money ?

That can be very easily done. My hon. friend says that the Minister of Inland Revenue knows something about it, as I know he does. Perhaps the Minister of Inland Revenue will explain to us the position of affairs as regards these two conflicting opinions in St. Hyacinthe.

My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue will certainly give me the benefit of his local knowledge of the facts, and it will be my duty and my pleasure to ask his advice. Before making up my mind, the matter will be thoroughly looked into. But my hon. friend must not forget that in questions of this kind I am not the master, I cannot buy a site without going before council, who will discuss the whole matter. I could not undertake to say that I will make choice of a certain site, that I would recommend this site or that site, because my colleagues might not agree with me. Master of the administration as I am, it may happen that my colleagues do not agree with me.

The usual course is to state what the building is going to cost. I think the minister is departing from a custom which prevailed during the time of his predecessors, of asking the town where an important building was to be put up, to furnish the site, or at least to pay a good share of the expense. That has been done in several towns in Ontario.
What towns ?

It seems to me it was done in London, I think it was done in Gananoque, and I think an offer was made by Brockville. But I know the previous Minister of Public Works made it a practice, when he intended to put up a public building in any city or town, to say to them : What are you going to do ? It will benefit your place, will you provide a site free, or pay a portion of the cost ? I think that might well be done. I think the minister is bound to give us the information in his estimates of what this building is going to cost, so that we may know to what we are committing ourselves.

As to the site, I cannot possibly say where it will be. I quite grant that I may be asked to say how much we will spend. I think that we will not spend more than $20,000 or $25,000 on that drill hall. We have not many drill halls. St. Hyacinthe is an important district. There is a good mili-

tary spirit now and I think it is only fair to give them a chance in developing it. That is the reason why a drill hall will be very well located there. I intend having plans prepared for a building costing about $20,000 or $25,000, a good deal less than some of the Ontario armouries cost. Perhaps we are spending a good deal there, but I do not think we should be reproached for that expenditure at all.
Then, I understand the hon. minister has not obtained his information from his architect, but that this is the amount that is in his mind.
Yes, we will spend that much and no more than $25,000.
That is based on the hon. gentleman's own judgment ?

I think we are entitled to some information from the hon. Minister of Public Works, or the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) on this question. Here is a question that has agitated the public mind in St. Hyacinthe for over two years. They are entitled to a drill hall and they know they would have had it some time ago had there not been a bitter discussion as to the site, and we are asked to-night to begin a work that will not cost less than $60,000 while leaving parliament and the people of St. Hyacinthe in the dark as to where that drill hall is to be located. If the hon. Minister of Public Works will allow me, I will read from the Liberal organ a short reference to that question, ' L'Union ' of St. Hyacinthe of the 11th April, 1901. It says this :
(Translation.) The ' Courier de St. Hyacinthe ' in its issue of the 8th instant published a short article which we reproduce here, for the information of our readers, who are anxious to be acquainted with all matters of interest to our city :
' From what has lately transpired, we have very good reason to believe that a sum of $60,000 is to be placed in the estimates for the erection of a drill hall on which work will be started this year in ward No. 5, and this with all due deference to Mr. Morison and other gentlemen who are opposed to it. It is further rumored that the sum. of $20,000 will, within a few days, be voted, to begin the work. The Dominion military authorities understand better the pressing needs of this city than some self-seeking gentlemen do, who rather than seeing the only ward of the city that is likely to make any substantial progress benefited by this improvement, would wantonly deprive the city of this boon.
Mr. TALBOT-(Translation). Shame !

What is my hon. friend (Mr. Talbot) saying ?
Mr. TALBOT-I said shame.

The hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about.
(Translation). We congratulate our contemporary upon this authentic piece of news

which was, no doubt, drawn from the copious fountain of official news for the district of St. Hyaeinthe ; and we, particularly congratulate him upon his promotion to the important position of official organ of the Dominion government. We have on former occasions pointed out the tendencies of this conservative organ.
With the ' Courrier ' we rejoice in the fact that the government have at last made up their minds to spend public money in St. Hyaeinthe.
As we could never bring ourselves to believe that there were to be found in this city self-seeking men who had an interest in seeing the city deprived of the important improvement which the ' Courrier ' promises us on behalf of the Dominion government, we can-rot endorse the following portion of the short paragraph published by our contemporary : ' We know that the only thing which did come under discussion was the purchase of a site by the city ; the intention being to give the municipal council the right of having their say in the choice of a site, the more so as the ratepayers of the city were being called upon to defray the cost of it. And to our mind, it was but fair and just that they should have done so.'
It seems to me that the subject of erecting a drill hall at St. Hyaeinthe, which is entitled to that improvement, and there is no objection to it whatever, is one on which we should have clear and definite information. We are ready to vote the amount required and there will be no making mistakes. It is a large amount that will be required to complete the building. We are entitled to know on behalf of that important section of the population who require a drill hall where it is going to be built before we vote this amount.
The hon. gentleman has just read an article from a Conservative paper. I do not intend to be guided by the advice it contains.
Which paper ?
' Le Courrier
I have read from ' L'Union
' L'Union ' has simply reproduced an article published in ' Le Courrier
And confirmed it.

Very well ; ' L'Union which is not very well pleased with some of us now, has thought fit to reproduce, an article from a Conservative paper. I do not intend to he guided by newspaper articles in the choice of a site for a military armoury. I intend to be guided by the ordinary rules of business. I hope my hon. friend does not object to whichever site it may be built on. Has he a choice to offer me ?
Are not the government brave enough to come and tell us in parliament where they are going to build it ?

Bravery has not much to do with this case ;
bravery is not in it at all. It is not a question of bravery ; it is a question of business. I will choose that site on the ordinary rules of business. I may have to go down there after the session is over. In the meantime I will ask parliament to have enough confidence in us to place this vote at our disposal. It is the first time since I have been in office that I remember of the opposition declining to vote money because a site was not chosen. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier belongs to the province of Quebec ; he should not ask us to deviate from the ordinary rules. The choice of a site is never made beforehand. I must get the money before choosing the site. I ask my hon. friend to think twice before placing any obstacle in the way of this vote. Suppose I were to go to council and to tell them that I had decided on a site. If council did not agree with me, I would be obliged to go elsewhere. Therefore, I am not in a position to state where the site will be.

I can understand the position of the hon. minister, but the government is not ruled altogether by the hon. Minister of Public Works, though I am prepared to admit that his views have very large importance. But, we have the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue who is from St. Hyaeinthe, and who knows that this controversy has been going on for the past two or three years. I think we are entitled to know from him what his views are upon the site of the drill hall at St. Hyaeinthe. It seems only fair. Why should he remain utterly silent ?

May I ask the hon. Minister of Public Works why he treats this matter, which is a Quebec matter, differently from the way in which he treats a Toronto matter when it comes up. When a vote is asked for dredging in Toronto harbour, the Minister of Public Works, and I think very justly, wants to know what Toronto is going to do. Toronto must have its money to do its share before he will do anything. When a drill hall had to be built the people of Toronto were obliged to plank down $100,000, or, at all events, to provide a site, and this matter was arranged before the Minister of Public Works condescended to put in an appropriation for the building of that drill hall. I will ask him why he makes this difference between the two provinces ?

I am not making any difference. It is the hon. member for Jacques Cartier who is himself making that difference. If my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) will be good enough to refer to the next page he will find several items for public buildings in Ontario, Clinton, Cobourg, Deseronto, Fort William, London, Sault Ste. Marie, Sarnia and Toronto Junction. In all of these cases the money is voted before the site is chosen. It is just as in this case. It is always done as I am doing it now. If my hon. friend who is a

sound business man will kindly remember what I am saying, my position is this. My recommendation does not always carry. Suppose 1 recommend one site in St. Hya-cinthe and my colleagues say no, I would be obliged to go elsewhere. It is always done just as I am now doing it.

While the hon. Minister of Public Works is speaking of proposed improvements in the province of Ontario perhaps he will not find fault with me if I mention the St. Catharines drill hall. In 1900 a contract was made and an amount placed in the estimates, which, however, was dropped on account of some such dispute as seemed to have occurred in St. Hyacinthe as to the location of the building. In that case St. Catharines bought the site and St. Catharines is paying for it. They are waiting for an appropriation in the estimates in order to take the deed. The city of St. Catharines is ready to hand over a cheque for $5,500 for the drill hall site, in order that the work may be carried out as contemplated by the item in the estimates for the year 1900. St. Catharines is in a border county, and is about the same size as St. Hyacinthe, and I am not unduly pressing the minister when I ask, why St. Catharines has not been treated as St. Hyacinthe has been. I think the drill hall site met with the approval of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) when he visited St. Catharines this last fall. He came there I believe on behalf of the Minister of Militia and Defence to inspect the site. Can the Minister of Public Works tell me if there will be a vote for the St. Catharines drill hall in the supplementary estimates 7

As to the supplementary estimates I am in the hands of my colleagues. It is a question of money and in questions of money the Minister of Public Works has a good deal of trouble at times. I cannot say anything as to the supplementary estimates. They have not been discussed with my colleagues, not one word.

What was pointed out to the Minister of Public Works was that St. Catharines, Toronto, and Gananoque, have provided the sites whereas St. Hyacinthe has not done so. Why is one place treated differently from the other ?
If the hon. gentleman will look at the list of public buildings in Ontario he will find that not one town of twenty furnished the site.

I have already cited three instances where towns supplied the site, and I am quite sure that I could find more if I went through the list. However, the principle is the same In one case the town is willing to provide the site and in the other case you do not even ask the town to do so.

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, it depends. Generally when the town gives the site the goveimment is asked to give more money and it does not save us anything. I know all about it. When the town is very anxious to get a public building the people come and say :	Now, Mr. Minister, if you are good enough, we will give you a chance to put up a fine public building and we will supply the site. You may rest assured that I am speaking gospel truth now. When they want an expensive building they make a pretense that they will give the site, and then it is rot always the best site in the town. We save nothing by it.

In reply to my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) I may say that I did not visit St. Catharines officially. I am one of the hon. gentleman's electors, and while in the city one day some members of the council asked me to look at the various sites. I quite agree with those who opposed the old site as chosen by the council and which was also declined by the minister. After looking at several sites which the council had in view, I certainly personally-if I can speak personally-approved very much of one or two of the sites shown me. I think they would make splendid sites for that building. I may say, as one of the hon. member's electors and knowing the importance of the city, that I would be very pleased indeed if the Minister of Public Works could see his way clear to give us a new drill hall. It is something that is needed in that city and district. I believe that the site which has been chosen by the council will be very suitable indeed, and that when a good building is placed upon it, it will be very creditable to the city.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

An armoury was built at Dundas, and just before the last election we were led to believe that a drill hall would be erected. I believe a start was made then, but after the election the matter dropped and nothing has been heard since. I would like to know if there will be a vote for that in the supplementary estimates 7

There is a general vote of $37,000 out pof which the amount necessary to complete the Dundas armoury will be taken.
Tbettord Mines-public building, $4,000.
Has the site been purchased?

Unfortunately I have been unable to secure a site. As in Marysville, the whole of the property is in the hands of the lumbermen and they have declined to sell me a site. They want me to take a lease for ninety years or something like that, but unless I can buy a site I shall not erect a building.
Will that building be occupied only for a post office ?
I intend there as elsewhere, to have a room set apart for an armoury. That is not a bad idea I think. There is a customs officer there and the building will be used [ by him.
What will the building cost to complete V
I intend erecting a cheap building to cost not more than $5,000.
What is the population of Thetford Mines ?
Four thousand I think. I have the figures here.
You may have the figures, but not the people on the place. The minister is a little extravagant in putting such a building in Thetford Mines.
The population is 5,000, if the census is not wrong.
You may find them there ten years from now if the place keeps growing. At present you will find them scarce.
In 1891 the population was 3,314. Surely the French Canadian boys have progressed to 5,000 now.
The population was more in 1891 than it was in 1892-3-4-5-6. The price of the mineral has been decreasing, and the people went away, but since 1898 they came back again.
It is all right, then.

It is all right, but they are not there.
Valleyfield public building, $10,000.
Has a site been chosen in this case ?
No, it has not.
Is it the intention of the government to purchase for this building a property belonging to Mr. Loy, the late member of this House ?

Surely the hon. member will not ask me to choose the site to-night. I may once more have to go to Valleyfield in a few days. But. joking aside, no choice of a site has been made as yet. Valleyfield is a thriving town, having to-day a population of 12,000. It is one of the most progressive towns in the province of Quebec, owing to the large industry which is so successfully carried on there.
Has the government received any offers of sites ?
No, I have not received any definite offer.
Any offer at all ?
Several suggestions have been made to me.
Has the property I refer to been suggested to the minister ?

I do not know that Mr. Loy owns any property there. One site has been suggested across the river near the mills, and a couple of sites have been suggested to me on this side of the canal. I have not yet made any choice whatever. My mind is altogether free and unbiased.
Has the site I refer to been offered or suggested to the minister ?
It has not been offered to me.
Is the minister able to say whether it has been suggested to him ?
I will not swear.
How much will this building cost ?
Between $20,000 and $25,000. Valleyfield in a short time will be a city, and we must give it a proper building-not large, but decent.

I would suggest to the minister that he follow the salutary custom of his predecessor, and induce some of these towns to contribute part of the cost or at least to furnish a site. I think a large town like Valleyfield should do so.
My hou. friend should not say it has been the custom or the policy of my predecessor. It may have been done on some occasions, but that has been the exception.

I was not speaking of the present government; but I do know that the hon. gentleman's predecessor, Sir Hector Langevin, as a rule-there may have been some exceptions-when an application was made from any town or village for a public building, almost invariably asked, ' what are you prepared to do ? furnish a site or contribute part of the cost,' and he generally got them to do something.

There is a statement in the department showing the number of public buildings in the country, and I make bold to say that when my hon. friend looks over that statement he will find that in not more than one case out of twenty have the towns contributed a dollar towards the cost of public buildings.
Will the hon. gentleman bring down that information ?

With pleasure.
-Mr. CLARKE. Is there no public building in Valleyfield, with a population of 10,000 or 12,000 ?
No, not one.

There seems to be more necessity for a public building in Valleyfield than in some of the other places which we hare been discussing.
Public buildings, Ontario-Clinton public building, $5,000.
What is this for ?
A post office and custom-house. The population is 3,000, and Clinton is a thriving town.
According to the census, the population is 2,547, against a population of 2,035 in 1891. It seems to be one of the Ontario towns that are going backward. What is the building going to cost ?
We have bought the site there from a good opponent of ours, Mr. A. W. Wilkie. We will spend more than $8,000 on the building.
This vote is additional to what was voted last year ?
Yes.

I think it will be in the recollection of the Minister of Public Works that he told the committee a year ago that this building was to be erected on a new plan. It was to be not only a post office, but a residence for the postmaster, and the plan of erecting cheap public buildings was to be started at Clinton. He certainly did not give the committee to understand that he was going to ask an additional $5,000 to what was voted last year, when it was believed that a site could be purchased for $1,000 and a building of sufficient importance, a substantial brick building, could be erected at a cost of about $5,000. I do not desire to quarrel with the minister about the style or cost of this particular building. But as the minister had decided that this building should be erected on a new plan, so as to be a model of what we could do in the way of cheap buildings, we certainly looked forward to seeing how this plan would work. We were all interested in the success of this experiment, as many counties in Ontario and the other provinces hoped to secure public buildings at the maximum cost of $5,000 or $6,000. But I am afraid the minister has forgotten his good intentions.

I am obliged to my hon. friend for he has just reminded me of what I forgot to mention. In this, as in the case of all public buildings we are erecting now, we intend having the postmaster reside in the building, which will be a great saving indeed. As to the exact cost of the building, it is difficult to say in advance. Last year I said it would not cost more than $5,000 or $6,000, but it may cost a couple of thousand more. The site cost more than we contemplated.
Is the postmaster to take charge instead of having a caretaker ?
Yes.
Will the hon. gentleman make any saving in the salary of the postmaster by having him reside in the building ?
We make a great saving by not having a caretaker. A caretaker costs generally $300 or $400 a year. When the postmaster acts as caretaker, we generally give him a small remuneration.
Do you propose to make him allowances for wood and light ?
Yes.

What process has a town to go through in order to secure a post office ? I find that we have voted $8,000 for a post office at Marysville. Also large sums for other towns, many of which have small populations as compared to Dun-das, which has never had a post office yet. The postal revenue of Dundas amounts to $4,345, while that of Marysville is only $1,398. At Dundas the money orders issued amount to $11,064 and at Marysville they are only $748. In Dundas the post office orders paid amount to $9,395 and in Marysville they are only $555. Yet Marysville Is getting a post office and Dundas is not. It seems to me the objections urged from this side tonight are very pertinent. Something more ought to be required of a town to entitle it to a public building than that it should send a representative to support the government. There ought to be some policy, based on population or revenue, which should be followed out, and not compel a locality to send a representative down to support thb government if it expects to be given a public building.

We are not so exacting as that. My hon. friend, who shows a good deal of ability in debate, will have to find stronger reasons to convince the House that it is necessary to have a public building in Dundas. But is there not a public building there already?
Dundas has no post office.

It has an armoury, on which we have spent a good deal of public money in the past. There ought to he some fairness even in public life. My hon. friend has already a public building, which has cost the country a large amount of money, and he now wants another.
AVhy not erect a post office attached to the drill hall, and have the two in the one building ?
The armoury was just started a few weeks before the election. A few bricks have been laid and nothing else done.

It will no doubt be completed yet.
Cobourg towards construction of armoury,

Mr. SPllOULE. What about that building ?
I am trying to find a site, but so far have not been able. Not having the site, I have not spent any money, which must be pleasant to the hon. gentleman.

I think that the system of voting money every year without using it, is entirely wrong. Unless it is clearly shown to the minister that it is absolutely necessary a public building should be erected in the near future, the vote should not be taken. You keep that vote standing from year to year and do nothing with it. If by the accidents of life, that constituency should become vacant, you can use this vote to carry the elections and it thus has a corrupting influence.

It is impossible for any minister to spend all the money in the estimates. To do so would require an immense staff to prepare plans and no minister would undertake'the work. Moreover we must not forget that we are only in the month of March, and the money was only voted last year. I have not had time to spend all the money which was put at my disposal.
Is this for the erection of a new building ?
I do not know. If I can get an old building which would suit our purpose, I would not build a new one.

The minister ought to know whether he is going to put up a new building or purchase an old one. Has he entered into any negotiations with reference to the purchase of an old building in the town of Cobourg ?
I have not negotiated with anybody but suggestions have been made and an old building has been talked of. I have not negotiated either for the price or the purchase.
What was it offered for?
I could not say. I have not paid much attention to that work.
Then the site has not yet been selected ?
No.
Carried.

No, not yet. I want to say here that I think the Minister of Public Works ought to be prepared with more definite information before he asks us to vote money. He evidently has come to no conclusion beyond the fact that he wants a building. Whether he will purchase an old one or build a new one, and, if the latter, what the site is to be, he does not know. If the hon. gentleman were in opposition he would be loud in his demands for more specific information before the money was voted. It has been usual to give this information, and to fail to give it now is to depart from a very salutary principle.

I do not think the hon. gentleman has put the case as fairly a# he generally does. Suppose a gentleman living in Ottawa were to make up his mind to remove to Toronto. He might decide to own a house there, and, for that purpose, to spend, let us say, $15,000. If he could find a suitable house at a fair price, he would buy, but if not be would purchase a site and put up a building of his own. The Minister of Public Works is in the same position. An armoury is wanted by the military authorities. If I can buy a property already in existence, suitable and in good condition and the price fair, why should I not buy it ? If I cannot find a suitable building at a fair price, I will have to find a site and erect a building. It is not fair to ask a minister in advance what he will do in a case of this kind, because he does not know. I have not been there and do not know much about the matter. When there is any difficulty I generally go to the place, try to understand the case and settle it.

I must confess that the minister is adopting a very strange course. I have been in this House a good many years, and have seen the Minister of Public Works in years gone by come here with plans and specifications and estimates, when he wished to get money for a new building. That system is being departed from and we are asked to vote large sums of money on the mere statement of the minister that he will decide afterwards what he will do with it. Why should not all these questions be settled before he asks us to vote these large sums of money ? It looks to me as

if there was a job in connection with it. I think we could turn to the files of the newspapers and show that the fact that there is a contemplated job is recognized by the editors of the papers in Coburg.
No.

Why should the hon. gentleman say, ' No ' so emphatically, when he tells us that he does not know what he is going to do ? I am afraid that some building will be unloaded on the country by political friends of the hon. gentleman. Why should the volunteers be put off with an old building ? It is impossible that an old building can be as suitable for the purpose as a new one. No matter what friends the hon. gentleman may have who happen to have an old building on their hands, that does not alter the fact that the volunteers there are entitled to a new building that will give them proper accommodation. I think the hon. minister should furnish us with more definite information before he asks us to vote $10,000, with the probability that lie will go up there and have an old building pawned off on him in exchange for the country's money.

I venture to tell the hon. gentleman that it has never been the custom of the department to bring plans' here when asking for votes of money. So, my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) is wrong in saying that this was the custom in the past. That point settled, let me say to the hon. gentleman also that I would not be a part to a job. I do not think the House can reproach me with knowingly having been a party to any dishonesty since I took office. I have tried to keep my hands clean, and I shall continue to do so in the future. I am sure that my hon. friend does not wish to import into the House party differences and difficulties and troubles ? I have received clippings of newspapers warning me of a job in this matter. There will be no job. There may be an old building there that is thought too little for this purpose. I have not seen it. If it is no good I will not purchase it. There are two parties in this business, the Department of Militia and Defence-and I would not think of buying a building for their use without their consent-and my own department, each department with its own architect and its own minister. There is no fear that there will be a job.
Will the hon. minister say whether it is intended to provide an armoury alone or an armoury and drill hall combined V

On Monday evening the estimates were brought down, and amongst the items we notice the sum of $10,000 for an armoury in Cobourg. This of course is a revote, as no expenditure has so far been made. This will of course bring up the

question of a site, and also make the Tammany politicians more active in working off the old Sutherland building on the government at an exorbitant price. All sensible persons will agree that the south-east corner of the market property is the best place for the new building, which will require to be well equipped and up-to-date. This site-
Now, here is a very important point

This site has we believe been offered by the town, is acceptable to the government, and will no doubt be the site, unless the speculating, grabbing politicians, who have been trying to work the Sutherland building deal, interfere, and fill their pockets with the public money, which was wisely intended for the benefit of the militia of this country in giving them a home and store-room for their arms.
Is that site offered by the town free ?
I understand so.

I read a day or two ago the extract the hon. gentleman has quoted. It was sent to me. I am very thankful to those who take so much interest in me. The extract is from a Conservative paper. I understand that there are people there who would like to see an expenditure of $30,000 or $40,000 for the armoury and drill hall combined. Before asking parliament for such a large amount of money I shall pause. I am asking for the modest sum of $10,000 for an armoury, which the military authorities here in Ottawa would have to approve.

The people are not so much interested in the hon. Minister of Public Works, perhaps, as in the proper expenditure of the public money for the purpose for which it is voted. I fail to see that he must bring himself so prominently before the public on every occasion, and complain that we are critising him. He is a servant of the people, and is there to spend their money for the people's interest. As far as I am concerned, I care but little where the money is spent, whether in a town in Quebec or in any other portion of this Dominion, if it is properly spent. I object to the people's money being spent for an old building belonging to any political heeler of this	or any other	government.Mr.	SPROULE.	The	minister	is asking
for $10,000, but he does not tell us what this building is going to cost including the site.
The	MINISTER	OF	PUBLIC	WORKS.
I shall not spend more than $15,000 for an armoury in Cobourg.

Of course he has no knowledge yet whether that will be used to purchase an old building or to build a new one.
The	MINISTER	OF	PUBLIC	WORKS.
I will decide the case on its merits after I have carefully investigated it.

Then I think before we vote this money the government should investigate the question on its merits, and give us the information, otherwise we are not justified in voting public money on his statement. I say again that no opposition is justified in allowing a vote of public money to pass unless we have some specific information of what the cost is going to be. Supposing we vote that money to-day, and the site should cost $10,000. The minister can give us no information now as to what it is going to cost. If my understanding is correct, the statement I saw in that paper was to the effect that the site is offered free,* but he is not prepared to accept it. But he wants so much money put at his disposal, and then he will use his own judgment.

I am asking the House to vote this money on the ordinary rule we have always followed. My hon. friends are trying to make political capital out of this, they are reading to the House articles from Conservative newspapers. It is their right, I do not complain. But it is our right and duty to stand by the ordinary rules of parliamentary procedure. The money has always been voted on the same principle to my predecessors in the Department of Public Works. I shall not tie my hands. Indeed my colleagues would not allow me to make any definite statement here, because it rests with them as much as with me. Before buying a site, before accepting even a tender, I have to report to my colleagues, and an Order in Council has to be passed. I am binding myself to a definite statement when I say that I shall not spend more than $15,000. I say again that I am asking parliament to vote this money on the ordinary principle of getting the money first and then deciding on the site, on my responsibility to the House.

The minister says some Conservative papers are complaining about it. Does he pretend to say that overtures were not made to him with regard to it ? He admitted a few minutes ago that suggestions were made. If a site is offered free, will he not tell us whether he will or not accept it, provided it is a good site and suitable for the purpose?

There is an old Latin axiom which says : Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes. I fear there is some foreign influence at work in this case. I am suspicious of presents offered to me from the other side of the House. I want to look at them carefully.

The government have at the present time in the town of Oobourg a site on which was erected a drill hall many years ago, and which was burnt down some twenty years ago or more. The militia authorities say that it is not a suitable site now upon which to erect a new armoury from the fact, that the ground is low and
cannot be drained, and that consequently the dampness would injure the arms that would be stored there. Two years ago when this question first came up some persons in the town assumed that the town would have to give a site. The town now owns a piece of property near the market square. They said if that were a suitable site they would be willing to give it. But it is open to the same objection as the site the government now owns, because the militia authorities say that the new guns they expect to get would be injured if stored on that site. The government will have this present site to sell for what it is worth, and can apply the money on the purchase of a new one. This site the government now owns was given to them by the town of Cobourg many years ago, and at the same time the town gave a grant of money to erect a drill hall, the one that was burnt down. But the government that had charge of it did not keep it insured, and when it burnt down it was a total loss. The town has lost the use of au armoury and drill shed during all these years, besides the money they contributed towards it twenty-five or thirty years ago. They have been agitating several years for this armoury, which is admitted on all hands to be an absolute necessity. I remember that during the session of 189(3, before the Conservative government went out of power, a deputation from the town of Cobojirg came down and interviewed the then Minister of Militia about this armoury. I think the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) was present at the time; and I myself was a member of the deputation. We then received a promise form the Minister of Militia that an appropriation for an armoury would be given, and it was reported by my opponent in the election that in the supplementary estimates of that session an appropriation was made for the purchase of a site. Whether that was true or not, I am unable to say, because, as hon. gentlemen will remember, the supplementary estimates that were prepared by the government at that time were never presented to parliament, owing to the fact that the House dissolved before they had aii opportunity of bringing them down. So I say that the preceding government was committed to the purchase of a site for this armoury and admitted that the old site was not a proper one. I may say that some of the arms that were stored in the old drill hall had to be moved before the place burned down because they were rusting on account of the dampness of the location. Now, with regard to these newspaper articles, I may tell the House what they mean. There is one local militia man who said to me : ' Don't have an old building under any circumstances, get a new one.' He said he had been told by officers of the department : ' You get the government started, and they will put you up a $30,000 building.' That is what they have in their mind, and

if tlie old building tbat is now suggested were purchased, then the total cost including repairs and equipment would come within the estimate, $12,000 or $13,000 at the outside.
Now, as far as I am concerned, I want no $30,000 spent for an armoury in my riding. I would not ash for it because I know the sentiment of the people would be against such an expenditure. I would consider it unnecessary. Ten thousand dollars for a building is what I would ask for and that with $2,000 for a site would be considered fairly sufficient. 1 realize that under present conditions it costs more to build than it did a few years ago. The Militia Department prepared a rough sketch some two years ago. It was handed over to the Public Works Department and it showed the accommodation they required in this armoury. If that is all the accommodation required, this old building that is referred to would give much more accommodation than the accommodation which they have pretented they require and it would not cost more than $10,000 or $12,000. The idea is a $30,000 building, but I do not think it is necessary to have any such expenditure.
What has the old building been used for 7
In the first place, before we had the post office at Cobourg, part of it was used for a custom-house. It has been used since that time as storehouse.
For ice ?

No, for grain. An American firm came over a few years ago and started growing what are known as fancy peas and it has been used as a storehouse for that purpose. At the present time people are living in it and one large portion is used as a ballroom. It has an excellent floor. In regard to the question of a site for a public building of that kind in out-town the number of desirable sites is very limited. We can get plenty of sites which all the military men object to because they a'-h too far out of town. I had a man in my office on Saturday who had heard of this proposal and who said that he had a site for the building. It is a good and desirable site if it suits the military men, but these sites are too far out for them. They want something on one of the principal streets near the centre of the town and in order to procure a site of that kind the department would be obliged to buy up a dwelling or a store or other business place which would make it very expensive. The Militia Department sent up two officers tof look after the available sites but they have not yet reported. Col. Montizambert, the district officer commanding from Kingston, and Col. Greer, of the 40th Regiment were the officers.
Deseronto public building, $16,000.
How much money has been spent on this building and how much will it cost to complete 7
The contract was awarded for $25,087. The probable cost of the building with the site, furniture, heating system, &c., will be $38,000.
The whole building finished will cost $38,000 7
Yes.	[DOT]
And it is all under contract 7
The fittings are not under contract.
Is the whole contract given to one contractor 7
No, I have just said that the contract for the erection of the building has been given for $25,687. There is nothing else given out by contract yet, because the building is not completed.
Is the remainder of the work to be given out by contract, or will it be done by day's work 7 The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. The heating will be given by contract.
Who is the contractor for the building 7

The contractor is Mr. Richard Sheehy, of Peterborough. The contract was given on the 25th June, 1901, to the lowest tenderer.
Dominion public buildings, renewals, improvements, repairs, etc., $10,000.
This is the general vote for all public buildings in Ontario.
Does that include furniture and all that sort of thing 7

Yes.
Fort William public building, $5,000.
A site has been given to us but we have not been able so far to go on with the work.
What is this for 7
Post office, custom-house, &c.
What is the estimated cost 7

I may say frankly that I have declined to go on with the work because the people of that town who are enterprising have asked me to put up a pretty expensive building. I

have waited to see how the cat would jump. They are very aggressive.
Oh.

Aggressive is a mild word. A site has beeu given. Every time that they approach me they say : We have given you a site; you must put up a large, fine building. I would rather not have a free site at times and have a little more freedom.

I do not think because a town gives a site that should trammel the minister. I think he should have perfect freedom to exercise his judgment as to the needs of the place and keep it within that no matter whether the site be given or not.

I do. I had supposed that a building that would cost $15,000 would be sufficient for Fort William unless the country goes ahead very quickly. There are large works going on, I may say, at that point. At this very moment the two railway companies that are centering there are contemplating large additions to their elevating power which will necessarily bring in population. I supposed that a $15,000 building would suffice.
Kingston Royal Military College-additional buildings, namely : gymnasium and hospital $6,000.
This is under contract and going on now.
I thought they had a gymnasium years ago.

This is to complete the work.
London drill hall and armoury, $10,000.
What is the explanation of that ?

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works to the question of the payment of architects fees. I notice the architect is paid 2i per cent on the work. There is a difference all through in the amounts paid for architects and clerks of works.
What place V

This is in the case of the London armoury. I was trying to get at the arrangements made for paying architects and clerks of works in different places. In London the architect is allowed 21 per cent on the cost of the armoury. He receives much less perhaps for his work in that case than another architect would receive for a work that would not cost half the amount that this one will cost.
In what other places ?

The architect for the London drill hall receives 24 per cent on the
estimated cost of $60,000, while the man in Nelson is paid $7 per day. It would be to that man's advantage to have the contractor employ few men in order to stretch the time for construction, because he is receiving $7 a day.

I am' sorry to say that in British Columbia, public works cost a fearful amount of money, nearly twice as much as in other provinces. It is the fact that the work in British Columbia is nearly 100 per cent dearer than in any other province, and it is not fair to make that comparison.

Well, take Vancouver, or Victoria, or Nelson, and in none of these places do you pay the same wages for the same services. In Kingston you pay a clerk of works $2.50 a day ; in Sarnia $3 and in St. Thomas $3. On what principle do you make that distinction. The only proper way is to act on the percentage system, and pay a lump sum. In my own town the architect goes down in the morning and examines the building, and sees that the work is going on. He receives $3 a day and he does not complain that few men are employed because the longer the work is going on the more he will receive. He was also the architect of the city hall for which he got a percentage of the estimated cost, and he went to the contractors and said ; You must put more men on the building, and he put them to the inconvenience of crowding the building with men in order that he might get his percentage quicker. The department is not taking the proper course here. They should first find out how long it should take to construct the building and give the contractors reasonable time.

We do so.
, Mr. INGRAM. No one will pretend that ' in the city of St. Thomas it takes a year * to construct an armoury worth $29,000.
i The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. It s takes a year to construct a building like 1 that.

Why, we have buildings
[DOT]	there that cost a great deal more and they did not take half the time to erect, but the
j architect got a percentage on the estimated t cost. These items that I have mentioned
-	will amount to a very large sum all over . Canada but other incidental expenses are r incurred through a building not being put
-	up within a reasonable length of time.
